title: Sabra and Shatila massacre in Israeli-controlled West Beirut
summary: From the evening of 16 September to the afternoon of 18 September 1982, two days after President-elect Bashir Gemayel's assassination, Lebanese Phalangist (Kataeb) militiamen entered the Sabra neighbourhood and the adjoining Shatila Palestinian refugee camp in West Beirut and killed Palestinian and Lebanese civilians over roughly 43 hours. Israeli forces, in West Beirut since 15 September, surrounded the camps, admitted the militia and fired illumination flares at night. Israel's Kahan Commission estimated 700 to 800 dead; the Palestinian Red Crescent reported more than 2,000; historian Bayan Nuwayhed al-Hout documented at least 1,300 named victims and estimated a maximum of 3,500. The UN Security Council condemned the killings in Resolution 521 on 19 September, and the General Assembly in December termed them an act of genocide. In February 1983 the Kahan Commission found Israel indirectly responsible and Ariel Sharon personally responsible, leading to his resignation; no Phalangist was prosecuted.

perspectives.framing: Describes the killings as a massacre of defenceless refugees carried out under Israeli protection after the fighters had left on US guarantees, and holds Israel and its commanders directly responsible alongside the Phalange.

Accepted the Kahan Commission's finding of indirect responsibility for failing to foresee and stop the militia, while stressing that the killings were committed by Lebanese Phalangists and denying that Israeli soldiers took part; some Israelis at the time called the inquiry a model of accountability.
Denied ordering a massacre, portraying the entry into the camps as a search for remaining fighters after Gemayel's assassination; the party has never accepted institutional responsibility.

Resolution 521 condemned 'the criminal massacre of Palestinian civilians in Beirut'; General Assembly resolution 37/123 D of 16 December 1982 resolved that the massacre was an act of genocide, a characterisation contested by Israel and several Western states.

title: Beirut bombings of 1983 and the emergence of Hezbollah
summary: On 23 October 1983 two truck bombs struck the barracks of the US Marine contingent at Beirut airport and a French paratroop base, killing 241 US service members and 58 French soldiers, according to their governments, along with several Lebanese civilians, the Marine Corps' largest single-day loss since Iwo Jima. On 18 April 1983 a car bomb had destroyed the US embassy in Beirut, killing 63 people. A group calling itself Islamic Jihad claimed the attacks; the United States attributed them to Lebanese Shia militants organised with Iranian Revolutionary Guard support, the network that became Hezbollah, which emerged after the 1982 Israeli invasion and published its founding open letter in February 1985. Hezbollah denies responsibility for the 1983 bombings. The multinational force withdrew in February 1984, the Israel-Lebanon agreement of 17 May 1983 collapsed, and Hezbollah's armed campaign against Israeli forces in southern Lebanon began.

perspectives.framing: Describes the barracks bombing as the deadliest terrorist attack on Americans before 2001, attributes it to Hezbollah acting with Iranian direction, and designated Hezbollah a foreign terrorist organisation in 1997.

Presents itself as an Islamic resistance movement born of the 1982 invasion to expel Israeli and Western forces from Lebanon, denies involvement in the 1983 bombings, and describes attacks on foreign troops in Lebanon as resistance to occupation.
Regards Hezbollah as an Iranian proxy created to wage war on Israel from Lebanon, and cites its attacks on Israeli forces from 1983 onward as justification for maintaining the security zone.
Acknowledges supporting the formation of Hezbollah as part of Islamic resistance to Israel and Western intervention, while denying operational responsibility for the Beirut bombings.

title: Israel withdraws to a self-declared 'security zone' in southern Lebanon
summary: Under a three-stage plan approved by the cabinet on 14 January 1985, Israel withdrew most of its forces from Lebanon, leaving Sidon in February, the Beqaa and Nabatiyeh areas in April, and completing the main pullback in early June 1985: The Washington Post reported on 7 June that the war was effectively over, although the army had missed its 6 June target and about 1,000 soldiers stayed behind. Israel retained a border strip three to twelve miles deep, called the security zone, held by an IDF garrison with the South Lebanon Army militia under General Antoine Lahad. The withdrawal, prompted by mounting casualties and domestic opposition, followed the collapse of the 17 May 1983 agreement and guerrilla attacks by Shia militias including Hezbollah. Lebanon and the United Nations regarded the zone as continued occupation contrary to Resolution 425; fighting continued there until Israel's full withdrawal in May 2000.

perspectives.framing: Presented the security zone as a limited defensive buffer to keep attackers away from Israel's northern border after the failure of the 1983 agreement, and the SLA as a local Lebanese partner.
Called the zone an occupation to be ended by resistance, and treated the 1985 withdrawal as the first fruit of its armed campaign; the SLA was described as a collaborationist militia.
The Lebanese government demanded complete Israeli withdrawal under Resolution 425 and did not recognise the SLA, while residents of the zone lived under a mixed Israeli-SLA administration.
UNIFIL reported that Israel's continued control of the zone prevented it from fulfilling its mandate, and the Security Council repeatedly reiterated its call for full withdrawal.

title: First Intifada begins after Jabalia road crash
summary: On 8 December 1987 an Israeli truck collided with vehicles carrying Palestinian workers at the Erez checkpoint, killing four residents of Jabalia camp. Many Gazans believed the crash was deliberate, and on 9 December protests spread from Jabalia across the Gaza Strip and then the West Bank; an Israeli patrol fired on demonstrators in Jabalia, killing a 17-year-old. The unrest became a sustained uprising, the First Intifada, combining stone-throwing, strikes, boycotts and local committees coordinated by a Unified National Leadership, met by Israeli curfews, mass arrests and deportations. Between 9 December 1987 and 13 September 1993, per B'Tselem, Israeli security forces killed about 1,070 Palestinians in the occupied territories (including 237 minors) and Israeli civilians killed 54 more, while Palestinians killed about 100 Israeli civilians and 60 security personnel; other tallies drawing on B'Tselem give 1,162 Palestinians killed by Israelis.

perspectives.framing: Describes the intifada ('shaking off') as a largely unarmed popular uprising against twenty years of Israeli occupation, and those killed as martyrs; Palestinian accounts treat the Jabalia crash as the spark for a revolt rooted in occupation, settlement and economic dependency.

Initially characterised the unrest as riots and disturbances orchestrated by the PLO and treated stone-throwing and petrol bombs as violent attacks on soldiers and civilians; Defence Minister Rabin's 'force, might, beatings' policy was defended as restoring order in Judea and Samaria and Gaza while avoiding live fire where possible.

B'Tselem, founded in 1989 in response to the uprising, documented killings by security forces, beatings, administrative detention, house demolitions and deportations and framed many of these as violations of international humanitarian law; it also recorded killings of Israelis and of Palestinians accused of collaboration.

title: Hamas founded by Muslim Brotherhood figures in Gaza
summary: In the first days of the intifada, leaders of the Muslim Brotherhood in the Gaza Strip, headed by Sheikh Ahmed Yassin with Abd al-Aziz al-Rantisi and others, formed Harakat al-Muqawama al-Islamiya (Islamic Resistance Movement), known by its acronym Hamas. Accounts cited by the Council on Foreign Relations and PBS describe a founding meeting in Gaza City on 9 December and a first communiqué issued under the Hamas name on 14 December 1987, the date most often given for the movement's founding. Hamas positioned itself as the Brotherhood's activist arm in the uprising, competing with the PLO-aligned Unified National Leadership and with Palestinian Islamic Jihad, and built on the Brotherhood's network of mosques, charities and the Islamic University of Gaza. Its emergence introduced an Islamist rival to the secular PLO that rejected negotiated partition of historic Palestine.

perspectives.framing: Presents itself as a Palestinian Islamic national liberation and resistance movement born of the intifada, dating its foundation to the uprising's first day and framing armed struggle (jihad) against Israeli occupation as a religious and national duty.

Regards Hamas as a terrorist organisation committed to Israel's destruction; Israeli accounts note that the authorities had earlier tolerated the Brotherhood's charitable network as a counterweight to the PLO and later outlawed Hamas in 1989.

Viewed Hamas as a competitor that stayed outside the Unified National Leadership and challenged the PLO's claim to be the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people, while sharing the goal of ending the occupation.

Later designated Hamas a foreign terrorist organisation (1997); US backgrounders describe it as an offshoot of the Muslim Brotherhood that combines social services, political activity and an armed wing.

title: Khalil al-Wazir (Abu Jihad) assassinated in Tunis
summary: In the early hours of 16 April 1988 a commando team landed by sea near Tunis and entered the home of Khalil al-Wazir, known as Abu Jihad, a co-founder of Fatah, deputy to Yasser Arafat and the PLO official overseeing the intifada from exile. According to Tunisia's complaint to the UN Security Council, the attackers shot dead a Tunisian gardener and two guards before killing al-Wazir in front of his wife and daughter. Tunisia blamed Israel; on 25 April the Security Council adopted Resolution 611 condemning the attack as a violation of Tunisian sovereignty, with the United States abstaining. Israel neither confirmed nor denied involvement until 2012, when the military censor cleared an interview with the Sayeret Matkal officer who led the raid, planned with the Mossad. Protests followed in the occupied territories.

perspectives.framing: Mourned Abu Jihad as a martyr and 'the engineer of the intifada', calling the killing an Israeli state assassination intended to decapitate the uprising's leadership; the November 1988 PNC session was dedicated to him.

Maintained official silence for 24 years; Israeli accounts published in 2012 describe al-Wazir as the commander responsible for attacks including the 1978 Coastal Road attack and frame the operation as a counter-terrorism strike against a legitimate military target.

perspectives.framing: Tunisia condemned an act of aggression on its territory; Resolution 611 called the attack a flagrant violation of the UN Charter and international law without naming Israel, and the United States abstained.

title: King Hussein severs Jordan's legal and administrative ties with the West Bank
summary: In a televised address on 31 July 1988, King Hussein announced that Jordan was dismantling its legal and administrative links with the West Bank, which it had annexed in 1950 and lost to Israel in 1967. He said Jordan would respect the wish of the PLO, recognised by the Arab League in 1974 as the sole legitimate representative of the Palestinian people, to establish an independent Palestinian state. The lower house of parliament, half of whose seats represented West Bank districts, had been dissolved the previous day; Jordan stopped paying about 21,000 West Bank civil servants and, according to Human Rights Watch, West Bank residents lost Jordanian citizenship under regulations issued soon afterwards. The decision removed the 'Jordanian option' from Israeli and American diplomacy and cleared the way for the PLO's November declaration of independence.

perspectives.framing: Presented the step as respecting Palestinian national aspirations and Arab consensus, ending Jordan's claim to sovereignty while preserving its custodianship of Muslim holy places in Jerusalem and its concern for Palestinian rights.
Welcomed the disengagement as recognition of its exclusive representation and as removing a rival claimant to the West Bank, enabling it to declare statehood over the occupied territories.

The Likud-led government, which rejected any Palestinian state, saw the removal of Jordan as a negotiating partner for Judea and Samaria as complicating the Camp David autonomy framework; Labor figures lamented the loss of the 'Jordanian option'.
Human Rights Watch later described the citizenship consequences as rendering many Palestinian-origin Jordanians stateless through opaque and arbitrary application of the 1988 regulations.

title: Hamas issues its founding charter (Covenant)
summary: On 18 August 1988 Hamas published the Covenant of the Islamic Resistance Movement, a 36-article charter setting out its identity, aims and worldview. The document defined Hamas as a wing of the Muslim Brotherhood in Palestine, declared all of Palestine an Islamic waqf (endowment) that no one may cede, rejected negotiated settlements and international conferences as contradicting its principles, and called for jihad to liberate the land; it also contained antisemitic passages and references to the Protocols of the Elders of Zion. Translations were later posted by the US Federation of American Scientists, Yale's Avalon Project and the Israeli Foreign Ministry, and the text was cited in UN Human Rights Council debates. In May 2017 Hamas issued a new political document accepting a state on the 1967 lines without formally revoking the 1988 charter.

perspectives.framing: Describes the charter as an expression of the movement's Islamic identity and its refusal to recognise the legitimacy of Israel's establishment on Palestinian land; later leaders have called it a historical document superseded in practice by the 2017 'Document of General Principles and Policies'.

Cites the covenant as proof that Hamas seeks the destruction of Israel and the killing of Jews, and argues the 2017 document did not change its fundamental goals; the Foreign Ministry titled its translation 'The Charter of Allah'.
Contrasted the charter's rejection of negotiation with the PLO's acceptance of a two-state solution, treating it as evidence of Hamas's refusal to join a unified national programme.

title: Palestine National Council declares the State of Palestine in Algiers
summary: At the close of its 19th session in Algiers on 15 November 1988, the Palestine National Council, chaired by Yasser Arafat, proclaimed the establishment of the State of Palestine with Jerusalem as its capital. The declaration, drafted by Mahmoud Darwish, invoked UN General Assembly Resolution 181 of 1947 as a source of legitimacy; an accompanying political communiqué accepted Security Council Resolutions 242 and 338 as the basis for an international conference, implicitly recognising Israel and endorsing a two-state outcome. The PNC vote was 253 in favour, 46 against and 10 abstaining. Dozens of states recognised Palestine within weeks, and on 15 December the UN General Assembly adopted Resolution 43/177 acknowledging the proclamation and adopting the designation 'Palestine' in place of 'PLO' in the UN system, by 104 votes to 2 with 36 abstentions.

perspectives.framing: Hailed the declaration as the culmination of the intifada and the exercise of the Palestinian people's right to self-determination, presenting acceptance of 242 and 338 as a historic compromise for peace on the 1967 lines.

Dismissed the declaration as a propaganda exercise by a terrorist organisation, noting the PNC's continued reference to armed struggle and its failure to explicitly recognise Israel or renounce the Palestinian National Covenant.

Judged the Algiers texts ambiguous and insufficient to open a dialogue, insisting on explicit acceptance of Israel's right to exist and an unambiguous renunciation of terrorism; it denied Arafat a visa to address the General Assembly in New York.

Acknowledged the proclamation in Resolution 43/177 and moved the December session to Geneva so that Arafat could speak, while affirming the need for Palestinian sovereignty over the territory occupied since 1967.

title: Arafat's Geneva statement opens a US-PLO dialogue
summary: After the United States refused Yasser Arafat a visa, the UN General Assembly moved its debate on Palestine to Geneva, where Arafat addressed it on 13 December 1988, calling for peace and saying he opposed terrorism in all its forms. Washington judged the speech insufficient. At a press conference on 14 December Arafat read a clarifying statement: the PLO accepted Security Council Resolutions 242 and 338, recognised the right of Israel to exist in peace and security, and 'totally and absolutely' renounced terrorism. Within hours Secretary of State George Shultz announced that the PLO had met US conditions and that the United States would open a substantive dialogue, with Ambassador Robert Pelletreau in Tunis as the sole authorised channel; the first meeting took place in Carthage two days later. The 13-year US ban on PLO contacts ended, though Israel objected.

perspectives.framing: Presented the Geneva statements as the Palestinian 'peace offensive' that translated the Algiers declaration into terms the world could accept, and the US dialogue as long-overdue recognition of the PLO as a negotiating partner.

Shultz said the PLO had accepted 242 and 338, recognised Israel's right to exist and renounced terrorism, so the US was 'prepared for a substantive dialogue'; officials stressed that US policy against a Palestinian state and support for Israel were unchanged.

Prime Minister Shamir's government called the US move a grave error, arguing that Arafat's words were tactical and that the PLO remained a terrorist organisation whose covenant called for Israel's destruction.

title: Bus 405 attack on the Tel Aviv-Jerusalem highway kills 16
summary: On 6 July 1989 a Palestinian passenger from the Gaza Strip, Abd al-Hadi Ghanim, seized the steering wheel of Egged bus 405 as it travelled from Tel Aviv to Jerusalem and forced it off Highway 1 into a ravine near Kiryat Ye'arim, where it caught fire. Sixteen people were killed, including two Canadians and an American, and 27 were injured, according to Israeli accounts; the attacker survived and was sentenced to 16 life terms. Palestinian Islamic Jihad claimed the attack, which Israeli sources describe as the first Palestinian suicide attack inside Israel. It was the deadliest single attack on Israelis during the First Intifada and led to tighter restrictions on Gaza workers entering Israel and calls in Israel for the death penalty. Ghanim was released to Gaza in the 2011 Shalit prisoner exchange.

perspectives.framing: Described the incident as a murderous terrorist attack on civilians and a sign that the intifada had spread lethal violence inside Israel's pre-1967 lines; survivors' groups have campaigned against the perpetrator's release.
Claimed the attack as a resistance operation and described Ghanim as a hero of the intifada; Islamic Jihad and Hamas later celebrated his release in the 2011 exchange.
B'Tselem counted the victims among Israeli civilians killed by Palestinians during the intifada and documented the subsequent collective measures imposed on Gaza residents.

title: Israeli police kill 17 Palestinians at the Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif
summary: On 8 October 1990, during the Sukkot holiday, thousands of Palestinians gathered at the Haram al-Sharif / Temple Mount after rumours that the Temple Mount Faithful group would lay a cornerstone for a new temple. Clashes broke out around mid-morning; stones were thrown towards the Western Wall plaza and Israeli police and border police used tear gas, rubber bullets and live fire. According to the Israeli Zamir commission and a B'Tselem report annexed to the UN Secretary-General's report, 17 Palestinians were killed; some Palestinian accounts put the toll at 21, with more than 150 Palestinians and about 20 Israelis injured. The Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 672 on 12 October condemning the violence and Resolution 673 on 24 October deploring Israel's refusal to receive a UN mission. Israel's commission found the police had faced mortal danger but faulted their preparation; no officers were charged.

perspectives.framing: Called the events the 'Temple Mount riots', describing an organised assault by thousands of stone-throwers on Jewish worshippers at the Western Wall; the Zamir commission concluded that police lives were in danger, and Israel rejected UN involvement as interference in its internal affairs and sovereignty in Jerusalem.

Described the 'Al-Aqsa massacre' as unprovoked killing of worshippers defending the mosque, demanded international protection for Palestinians under occupation and used it to press for UN action during the Gulf crisis.

Resolution 672 condemned the acts of violence committed by Israeli security forces, expressed alarm at the loss of life and asked the Secretary-General to send a mission; Resolution 673 deplored Israel's refusal to receive it.

B'Tselem's investigation, transmitted to the Security Council, disputed the official account of an ambush, finding that police had opened fire on retreating crowds and used live ammunition disproportionately.

title: Iraq fires Scud missiles at Israel during the Gulf War
summary: In the early hours of 18 January 1991, the day after the US-led coalition began air strikes on Iraq, Iraq launched the first of a series of modified Scud missiles at Israel, striking Tel Aviv and Haifa. Over the following five weeks about 39 Scuds were fired at Israel, according to an MIT Defense and Arms Control Studies paper and Israel's Defence Ministry; most fell in the Tel Aviv area, including a heavy hit on Ramat Gan. Israelis were issued gas masks and sealed rooms amid fears of chemical warheads, which were never used. The same paper recorded two people killed directly and about a dozen deaths from heart attacks or misuse of gas masks. Under US pressure, and with Patriot batteries deployed by American crews, the Shamir government did not retaliate, preserving the Arab members of the coalition. The attacks ended with the late-February ceasefire.

perspectives.framing: Framed the missile strikes as unprovoked aggression against civilians by a regime that had threatened to 'burn half of Israel', and its restraint as a strategic sacrifice made at Washington's request; the episode strengthened arguments for missile defence and for Israel's security concerns in later talks.
Presented the attacks as striking the 'Zionist entity' in retaliation for the coalition bombing, aiming to draw Israel into the war and split Arab states from the US-led coalition.
Praised Israel's 'remarkable restraint', rushed Patriot batteries and crews to Israel and pressed Jerusalem not to intervene so as to keep Egypt, Syria and Saudi Arabia in the coalition.

Arafat's public alignment with Saddam Hussein and scenes of Palestinians cheering the Scuds were framed by the PLO as solidarity against Western intervention, but cost it Gulf funding and weakened its diplomatic position.

title: Madrid Conference opens direct Arab-Israeli negotiations
summary: From 30 October to 1 November 1991 the Madrid Conference, co-sponsored by the United States and the Soviet Union and opened by Presidents George H. W. Bush and Mikhail Gorbachev, brought Israel into the first direct public negotiations with Syria, Lebanon and a joint Jordanian-Palestinian delegation. Secretary of State James Baker had made eight trips to the region after the Gulf War to secure attendance; Israel, led by Yitzhak Shamir, agreed on condition that the PLO was excluded and that Palestinians from the occupied territories, headed by Gaza physician Haidar Abdel Shafi, took part within Jordan's delegation. The invitation letter envisaged two tracks: bilateral talks on the basis of Resolutions 242 and 338 and multilateral working groups on regional issues. Bilateral negotiations began in Madrid on 3 November and continued in Washington through 1993, with the Palestinian track producing little before the secret Oslo channel.

perspectives.framing: Bush presented the conference as a historic opportunity created by the Gulf War to trade 'territory for peace' through direct talks, insisting the US would not impose a settlement.

Shamir framed participation as talks on peace and autonomy without preconditions, rejected territorial withdrawal and land-for-peace in his speech, and stressed that the PLO and East Jerusalem residents were excluded.

Abdel Shafi's address called for an end to occupation and settlement and Palestinian self-determination; the PLO, formally excluded, directed the delegation from Tunis and viewed Madrid as recognition of Palestinians as a party.
Foreign Minister Farouk al-Sharaa attended to recover the Golan Heights on the basis of full withdrawal for full peace and used his speech to denounce Shamir's record.

title: Yitzhak Rabin's Labor Party wins Israeli general election
summary: In the Knesset election of 23 June 1992 the Labor Party under Yitzhak Rabin, who had defeated Shimon Peres for the leadership in February, won 44 of 120 seats with about 34.7 per cent of the vote, while Yitzhak Shamir's Likud fell to 32 seats, according to the Israel Democracy Institute. Turnout was about 77 per cent. Labor, Meretz (12 seats) and the ultra-Orthodox Shas party formed a coalition, with the outside support of five Arab-party Knesset members giving Rabin a blocking majority of 61. Rabin took office as prime minister and defence minister on 13 July with Peres as foreign minister, promising to reach an agreement on Palestinian autonomy within six to nine months and to curb 'political' settlements. The change of government ended the Bush administration's dispute with Shamir over loan guarantees and settlement building and enabled the secret Oslo channel.

perspectives.framing: Rabin presented the result as a mandate to change national priorities, pursue peace with the Palestinians and Arab states from a position of strength and redirect resources from settlements to immigrant absorption and infrastructure.

Shamir and Likud attributed the defeat to internal splits and US pressure, warned that Rabin would concede parts of the Land of Israel, and argued that the coalition depended on Arab votes and lacked a Jewish majority.

Institute for Palestine Studies commentary saw the election as opening possibilities in the Washington talks while cautioning that Rabin's positions on Jerusalem, settlements and statehood differed from Likud's mainly in style.

The Bush administration welcomed the outcome and soon approved $10 billion in loan guarantees after Rabin agreed to freeze new settlement construction, treating the new government as a partner for the Madrid process.

title: Israel deports 415 Hamas and Islamic Jihad members to Marj al-Zuhur
summary: After Hamas members abducted and killed border police sergeant Nissim Toledano on 13-15 December 1992, following the killing of five other Israeli security personnel that month, the Rabin government ordered the temporary deportation of 415 Palestinians identified as Hamas and Islamic Jihad activists from the West Bank and Gaza Strip. On 17 December, after the High Court of Justice lifted an injunction, they were bused blindfolded into Lebanon for one or two years. Lebanon refused to admit them, so they camped at Marj al-Zuhur north of Israel's self-declared security zone; B'Tselem called it the largest single deportation since 1967. On 18 December the Security Council unanimously adopted Resolution 799 condemning the deportations as a breach of the Fourth Geneva Convention and demanding the deportees' return. Israel agreed on 1 February 1993 to repatriate 101 and halve the others' terms; most returned by December 1993.

perspectives.framing: Rabin described the deportations as a temporary, lawful measure against 'inciters and organisers' of Hamas terrorism after a wave of killings, rather than punishment of individuals for specific acts, and rejected the applicability of the Fourth Geneva Convention's deportation ban.

Treated the expulsion as proof of Israel's brutality and turned the tent camp into a media stage and 'university', framing the deportees as steadfast resisters; Hamas scholars later describe Marj al-Zuhur as a milestone in the movement's rise.

Resolution 799 strongly condemned the deportation of 'hundreds of Palestinian civilians', reaffirmed the Fourth Geneva Convention's application to the occupied territories including Jerusalem and demanded their safe and immediate return.

B'Tselem and Human Rights Watch called the mass deportation a grave violation of international humanitarian law carried out without due process, noting that many deportees were not accused of violence.

title: Operation Accountability: seven-day Israeli offensive in southern Lebanon
summary: From 25 to 31 July 1993 Israel carried out Operation Accountability, known in Lebanon as the Seven-Day War, after Hezbollah and PFLP-General Command attacks killed Israeli soldiers in the occupied 'security zone' and Hezbollah rockets hit northern Israel. Prime Minister Rabin ordered air, artillery and naval strikes on villages across southern Lebanon with the declared aims of striking Hezbollah, denying it a base and driving civilians north to pressure Beirut and Damascus to restrain it. Lebanese and human-rights sources cited by the Economic Cooperation Foundation put the dead at about 118-130 Lebanese, mostly civilians, with roughly 500 wounded; contemporary estimates cited in Israeli and Lebanese accounts spoke of up to 300,000 displaced. Hezbollah fire killed two Israeli civilians and one soldier, per the IDF. US Secretary of State Warren Christopher brokered an unwritten understanding on 31 July under which both sides agreed not to target civilians.

perspectives.framing: Rabin presented the operation as holding Lebanon and Syria accountable for Hezbollah attacks on Israeli troops and towns, stating openly that displacing residents was intended to press Beirut to act; the IDF describes it as a response to Katyusha fire on the Galilee.

Cast its rocket fire and attacks as legitimate resistance to Israel's occupation of southern Lebanon and claimed that the July understandings recognised its right to fight Israeli forces inside Lebanon.
Condemned the bombardment as aggression against civilians and infrastructure, appealed to the Security Council and highlighted the mass flight of villagers towards Beirut.

Human Rights Watch later criticised both Israel's deliberate targeting of civilian areas to create displacement and Hezbollah's indiscriminate rocket fire on Israeli towns as violations of the laws of war.

title: Israel and the PLO exchange letters of mutual recognition
summary: On 9 September 1993, after months of secret Norwegian-hosted talks in Oslo, Yasser Arafat signed a letter to Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin in Tunis stating that the PLO recognised the right of the State of Israel to exist in peace and security, accepted Security Council Resolutions 242 and 338, committed itself to a peaceful resolution of the conflict, renounced terrorism and other acts of violence, and undertook to submit to the Palestine National Council the changes needed to remove clauses of the Palestinian National Covenant inconsistent with these commitments. In a separate letter to Norwegian foreign minister Johan Jorgen Holst, Arafat pledged to call for an end to intifada violence. Rabin's reply in Jerusalem recognised the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people and agreed to negotiate with it. The exchange made possible the signing of the Declaration of Principles in Washington on 13 September.

perspectives.framing: Rabin and Peres described recognition of the PLO as a calculated risk that turned an enemy into a negotiating partner, stressing that Israel recognised the organisation, not a state, and conditioned progress on an end to violence and revision of the Palestinian Covenant.

Arafat presented Israel's recognition as the PLO's greatest diplomatic achievement, confirming its status as sole legitimate representative and opening the road to a Palestinian state; critics inside the PLO and Hamas denounced the letters as capitulation and recognition of Israel without reciprocity on statehood.
Rejected the mutual recognition and the subsequent Oslo Accords as a betrayal that surrendered most of Palestine, and vowed to continue armed resistance.

Washington, which had been sidelined by the Oslo channel, immediately resumed its dialogue with the PLO and hosted the Washington signing; Norway framed the exchange as proof that back-channel facilitation could break deadlocks.

title: Israel and the PLO sign the Oslo Declaration of Principles
summary: On 13 September 1993 Israel and the Palestine Liberation Organization signed the Declaration of Principles on Interim Self-Government Arrangements on the South Lawn of the White House. Israeli Foreign Minister Shimon Peres and PLO official Mahmoud Abbas signed the text in the presence of Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin, PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat and US President Bill Clinton, after which Rabin and Arafat shook hands. The declaration followed secret talks in Oslo, Norway, and an exchange of letters of mutual recognition days earlier. It set out a five-year transitional period of Palestinian interim self-government in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, beginning with an Israeli withdrawal from the Gaza Strip and the Jericho area, elections to a Palestinian Council, and permanent-status negotiations on Jerusalem, refugees, settlements, security and borders based on Security Council Resolutions 242 and 338.

perspectives.framing: The Rabin government presented the declaration as a historic breakthrough that secured PLO recognition of Israel and a renunciation of terrorism, while deferring Jerusalem, settlements and statehood to permanent-status talks and preserving Israeli responsibility for overall security.

The PLO leadership framed the accord as the first step towards ending the occupation and achieving an independent Palestinian state with Jerusalem as its capital, and as Israeli recognition of the PLO as the representative of the Palestinian people.

Hamas, Islamic Jihad and PFLP rejected the accord as a capitulation that surrendered most of historic Palestine and postponed refugees and Jerusalem, and refused to recognise the resulting self-government arrangements.
Likud and settler groups condemned the agreement as a dangerous concession to a terrorist organisation that endangered Israeli security and the Jewish presence in Judea and Samaria.
The Clinton administration hosted the ceremony and described the declaration as a historic act of reconciliation that the United States would support through aid and continued mediation.

location: Cave of the Patriarchs / Ibrahimi Mosque, Hebron, West Bank
title: Cave of the Patriarchs / Ibrahimi Mosque massacre in Hebron
summary: On 25 February 1994, during Ramadan, Baruch Goldstein, an Israeli settler physician from Kiryat Arba and supporter of the Kach movement, opened fire with an assault rifle on Muslim worshippers at dawn prayers in the Ibrahimi Mosque at the Cave of the Patriarchs in Hebron. He killed 29 worshippers and wounded about 125 before being overpowered and beaten to death, according to accounts reported by The Times of Israel and the Institute for Palestine Studies; Palestinian sources such as WAFA count more than 50 dead when those killed in subsequent protests are included. The Israeli government condemned the attack, outlawed Kach and appointed the Shamgar Commission of inquiry. Security Council Resolution 904 of 18 March 1994 condemned the massacre and led to the Temporary International Presence in Hebron. Israel-PLO talks were suspended for several weeks.

perspectives.framing: Prime Minister Rabin condemned the killings as the act of a 'degenerate murderer' outside the Israeli mainstream, banned Kach and Kahane Chai, and set up a state commission of inquiry, while rejecting Palestinian demands to remove the Hebron settlers.

The PLO called the attack a massacre that exposed the danger of armed settlers, suspended negotiations, and demanded the evacuation of settlements in Hebron and international protection for Palestinians.
Hamas described the attack as a Zionist massacre of worshippers and announced retaliation; its first suicide bombings inside Israel in April 1994 were declared to be revenge for Hebron.

Security Council Resolution 904 strongly condemned the massacre, called on Israel as the occupying Power to disarm settlers and prevent settler violence, and endorsed a temporary international presence in Hebron.

title: Gaza-Jericho Agreement signed in Cairo, creating the Palestinian Authority
summary: On 4 May 1994 Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat signed the Agreement on the Gaza Strip and the Jericho Area in Cairo, witnessed by the United States, Russia and Egypt. Implementing the first stage of the 1993 Declaration of Principles, it provided for the withdrawal of Israeli forces from most of the Gaza Strip and from the Jericho area, the transfer of civil and internal-security powers to a 24-member Palestinian Authority, the deployment of a Palestinian police force, and the release of Palestinian prisoners. Annexes covered security arrangements, civil affairs, legal matters and economic relations, incorporating the Paris Protocol on economic relations signed a week earlier. Israel retained control of settlements, military installations, external security and border crossings. According to the UN, the Israeli withdrawal from the specified areas was completed on schedule in May 1994.

perspectives.framing: Israel presented the agreement as the 'Gaza and Jericho first' implementation of Oslo, transferring responsibility for a densely populated and costly area while retaining overall security control, the settlements and the borders.

The PLO framed the Cairo agreement as the first exercise of Palestinian national authority on Palestinian soil and a stepping stone toward independence, while criticising Israel's retained powers and the small size of the Jericho enclave.
Egypt, as host and witness, portrayed the signing as vindication of its own peace with Israel and of its mediating role in the Arab-Israeli conflict.
Hamas rejected the agreement as a surrender that turned the PLO into an Israeli security subcontractor, and vowed to continue armed resistance.

title: Yasser Arafat returns to Gaza after 27 years in exile
summary: On 1 July 1994 PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat crossed from Egypt into the Gaza Strip at Rafah, his first return to Palestinian territory since leaving the West Bank in 1967. Under the Gaza-Jericho Agreement, Israeli forces had withdrawn from most of the Gaza Strip and the Jericho area in May and a Palestinian police force had deployed. Arafat was driven to Gaza City, where he addressed a crowd that press reports put in the tens of thousands, and days later visited Jericho, where the Palestinian Authority was sworn in. He established the seat of the new Authority in Gaza. Israeli opponents of the accords protested the visit, and Hamas supporters boycotted the welcome, but The Washington Post and other outlets described the return as the symbolic start of Palestinian self-rule.

perspectives.framing: Palestinian officials and WAFA describe the day as the triumphant homecoming of the national leader and the beginning of building state institutions on Palestinian land.

The Rabin government treated the visit as a contractual consequence of the Cairo agreement and stressed that Arafat's authority was limited to the autonomous areas under Israeli overall security responsibility.
Likud and settler leaders denounced the return as the entry of a terrorist leader to the gates of Israel and staged protests.
Hamas stayed away from the welcome ceremonies and characterised the Authority as a product of a flawed agreement that legitimised the occupation.

location: Wadi Araba / Arava border crossing, Israel-Jordan
title: Israel and Jordan sign the Wadi Araba peace treaty
summary: On 26 October 1994 Israel and Jordan signed a Treaty of Peace at the Wadi Araba (Arava) border crossing north of Eilat and Aqaba. Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and Jordanian Prime Minister Abdul Salam al-Majali signed, with King Hussein, Israeli President Ezer Weizman and US President Bill Clinton, who witnessed the treaty, in attendance. It followed the Washington Declaration of 25 July 1994, which had ended the state of belligerency. The treaty delimited the international boundary along the Jordan and Yarmouk rivers and the Arava, with special arrangements for the Baqura/Naharayim and Ghumar/Zofar areas, allocated Jordan and Yarmouk water shares, established diplomatic relations, and committed both states to cooperation on trade, tourism and security and to preventing their territory from being used for attacks on the other. Jordan became the second Arab state, after Egypt, to make peace with Israel.

perspectives.framing: Israel hailed the treaty as a 'warm peace' with its longest border neighbour, securing its eastern frontier and recognising Jordan's special role at Muslim holy sites in Jerusalem pending permanent-status talks.

King Hussein presented the treaty as recovering Jordanian land and water rights and securing the kingdom's future, while Jordanian opposition and professional associations rejected normalisation and called it a 'cold peace'.

The PLO welcomed the peace but objected to the clause giving Jordan a special role over Islamic holy places in Jerusalem, insisting that Jerusalem was a Palestinian matter for final-status negotiations.
The Clinton administration described the treaty as a milestone toward a comprehensive regional peace and offered Jordan debt relief and military assistance.

location: Beit Lid junction, near Netanya, Israel
title: Double suicide bombing at Beit Lid junction
summary: On the morning of 22 January 1995 two Palestinian suicide bombers detonated explosives about three minutes apart at a crowded bus stop at the Beit Lid (Sharon) junction near Netanya, where soldiers were waiting for transport back to their bases after the weekend. The second blast struck those who had rushed to help the wounded. Palestinian Islamic Jihad claimed responsibility, saying the bombers came from the Gaza Strip; it was the group's first suicide attack inside Israel. The Washington Post reported 19 dead the following day, while the Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs lists 20 soldiers and one civilian killed and 66 wounded. Israel sealed the West Bank and Gaza Strip, Prime Minister Rabin raised the idea of physical separation from the Palestinians, and the attack intensified Israeli debate over continuing the Oslo process.

perspectives.framing: Israel described the bombing as a terrorist massacre of young soldiers, demanded that the Palestinian Authority crack down on Islamic Jihad and Hamas, and imposed a closure on the territories.
Islamic Jihad claimed the attack as a 'martyrdom operation' against occupation soldiers and as retaliation for the killing of its members, rejecting the Oslo accords.
Yasser Arafat condemned the attack and ordered arrests of Islamic Jihad activists in Gaza, while objecting that closures collectively punished Palestinians.

title: Oslo II Interim Agreement divides the West Bank into Areas A, B and C
summary: On 28 September 1995 Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin and PLO Chairman Yasser Arafat signed the Israeli-Palestinian Interim Agreement on the West Bank and the Gaza Strip at the White House, witnessed by the United States, Russia, Egypt, Jordan, Norway and the European Union. Known as Oslo II, the agreement, initialled in Taba four days earlier, extended Palestinian self-government beyond Gaza and Jericho. It divided the West Bank into Area A, where the Palestinian Authority held civil and internal-security powers; Area B, with Palestinian civil control and Israeli overriding security responsibility; and Area C, under full Israeli control. Israel undertook to redeploy from six West Bank cities and hundreds of villages ahead of elections for a Palestinian Council, with further redeployments to follow. Hebron received special arrangements. The interim period was to end with a permanent-status agreement by May 1999.

perspectives.framing: The Rabin government presented Oslo II as ending Israeli rule over most Palestinians while keeping security control of settlements, the Jordan Valley and Area C, and insisted the Palestinian entity would be less than a state.

The PLO framed the agreement as extending Palestinian sovereignty over its cities and setting a timetable toward a state, while critics within Fatah noted that Area A covered only a small share of the West Bank.

Likud and settler groups denounced the agreement as a surrender of parts of the Land of Israel; the Knesset ratified it by only 61 votes to 59 amid heated protests in which Rabin was labelled a traitor.
Hamas rejected Oslo II as a fragmentation of Palestinian land into isolated enclaves that entrenched occupation, and continued attacks on Israelis.

location: Kings of Israel Square (now Rabin Square), Tel Aviv
title: Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin assassinated at Tel Aviv peace rally
summary: On the night of 4 November 1995 Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin was shot twice at close range by Yigal Amir, a 25-year-old Israeli law student and religious nationalist opposed to the Oslo accords, as he left a rally in support of the peace process attended by more than 100,000 people in Kings of Israel Square, Tel Aviv. Rabin died at Ichilov Hospital shortly afterwards. Amir was arrested at the scene, confessed, and was sentenced to life imprisonment. It was the first assassination of an Israeli prime minister. Shimon Peres became acting prime minister, and world leaders including King Hussein of Jordan and President Hosni Mubarak of Egypt attended the funeral on Mount Herzl on 6 November. The killing followed months of incitement against Rabin over Oslo II and deepened divisions within Israeli society.

perspectives.framing: Israel's leadership mourned Rabin as a soldier and statesman murdered by a Jewish extremist for pursuing peace, and pledged to continue the Oslo process; the Shamgar Commission later examined security failures.
Likud and religious-nationalist leaders condemned the murder while rejecting accusations that their campaign against the accords had created the climate for it.
Yasser Arafat described Rabin as a partner in peace and expressed fear that the assassination would derail implementation of the interim agreement.
The General Assembly held a special session at which speakers expressed shock and urged that the peace process for which Rabin had worked continue.

location: Jaffa Road, Jerusalem (also Ashkelon and Tel Aviv)
title: Wave of Hamas suicide bombings in Jerusalem, Ashkelon and Tel Aviv
summary: Between 25 February and 4 March 1996 Hamas carried out four suicide bombings inside Israel, which it said avenged the killing of its bomb-maker Yahya Ayyash in January. On 25 February a bomber destroyed a No. 18 bus on Jaffa Road in Jerusalem, killing 26 people (17 civilians and nine soldiers) according to the Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs; the same morning a bomber killed one soldier at a hitch-hiking post in Ashkelon. On 3 March a second No. 18 bus was bombed on Jaffa Road, killing 19, and on 4 March a bomber at Tel Aviv's Dizengoff Center killed 13 people, with CNN reporting 14 dead. In total about 59 people were killed and well over 100 wounded. Israel closed the territories, Prime Minister Peres declared 'war' on Hamas, and world leaders convened the Sharm el-Sheikh Summit of Peacemakers on 13 March.

perspectives.framing: The Peres government called the bombings terrorist massacres of civilians, imposed a full closure, demanded that the Palestinian Authority dismantle Hamas's military wing, and framed the response as a war on terrorism.

Hamas's military wing claimed the attacks as 'martyrdom operations' in revenge for the assassination of Yahya Ayyash and as resistance to occupation, while some political leaders offered a conditional halt.
Yasser Arafat condemned the bombings, arrested hundreds of Hamas activists and outlawed its armed wing, but protested that the closure devastated the Palestinian economy.
The Clinton administration condemned the attacks, co-hosted the Sharm el-Sheikh summit against terrorism and pledged support for Israeli security and for Peres's government.

title: Operation Grapes of Wrath and the shelling of the UN compound at Qana
summary: From 11 to 27 April 1996 Israel conducted Operation Grapes of Wrath, a campaign of air strikes and artillery fire across southern Lebanon and Beirut aimed at pressing Hezbollah and the Lebanese government to halt Katyusha rocket fire on northern Israel. Human Rights Watch documented some 600 air raids and 25,000 shells, and it and Amnesty International reported around 154 civilians killed and 351 injured in Lebanon, with roughly 400,000 people displaced after Israeli warnings to evacuate villages. On 18 April Israeli artillery struck the UNIFIL Fijian battalion compound at Qana, where about 800 civilians had sought shelter, killing 106 people according to the United Nations. A UN investigation concluded it was unlikely the shelling was the result of technical or procedural errors; Israel said it was responding to Hezbollah fire from nearby. US-brokered understandings announced on 26 April ended the fighting.

perspectives.framing: Israel described the operation as a defensive response to Hezbollah rocket attacks on Kiryat Shmona and Galilee, said the Qana deaths were a tragic error caused by targeting Hezbollah fighters firing from near the base, and rejected the UN report's conclusions.
Hezbollah framed its rocket fire as resistance to Israeli occupation of southern Lebanon and retaliation for civilian deaths, and called Qana a deliberate massacre.
Lebanon condemned the operation as aggression against its sovereignty and civilians and sought Security Council action and compensation for the Qana victims.

The Secretary-General's investigation, led by General Franklin van Kappen, found it unlikely that the shelling of the compound was due to gross technical or procedural errors, while noting Hezbollah fired from near the base; the Secretary-General deplored the loss of life.

Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International documented unlawful killings and argued Israel's evacuation orders and indiscriminate shelling violated the laws of war, while also criticising Hezbollah's rocket fire at Israeli civilians.

title: Benjamin Netanyahu narrowly defeats Shimon Peres in first direct vote for PM
summary: On 29 May 1996 Israelis voted for the first time in a direct election for prime minister alongside the Knesset ballot. Likud leader Benjamin Netanyahu, who had campaigned against the Oslo accords under the slogan of 'peace with security' after the spring suicide bombings, defeated Labour's Shimon Peres by 50.5 to 49.5 percent, a margin of about 29,500 votes, according to the Israel Democracy Institute and CNN. Likud-Gesher-Tzomet won 32 Knesset seats to Labour's 34, and Netanyahu formed a coalition of 66 members with religious and immigrant parties in June. The result ended the Labour government that had negotiated Oslo I and II. Netanyahu pledged to honour signed agreements but to condition further redeployments on Palestinian security performance and to oppose a Palestinian state, slowing implementation of the interim agreement.

perspectives.framing: Netanyahu presented his victory as a mandate for 'peace with security', reciprocity from the Palestinian Authority and opposition to dividing Jerusalem or establishing a Palestinian state.
Labour attributed its defeat to the Hamas bombings and warned that the new government would freeze the peace process.
Palestinian officials voiced alarm at the election of a leader who had opposed Oslo, while stating they would hold Israel to its signed commitments.
The Clinton administration, which had visibly favoured Peres, said it would work with the new government and urged continued implementation of the agreements.

location: Old City of Jerusalem, spreading to the West Bank and Gaza Strip
title: Western Wall tunnel opening triggers deadly clashes across the territories
summary: Overnight on 23-24 September 1996 the Israeli government opened a new exit from the Western Wall tunnel onto the Via Dolorosa in Jerusalem's Muslim Quarter, near the Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif. Palestinian protests began in Jerusalem on 24 September and spread over the following days to Ramallah, Bethlehem, Nablus, Gaza and other areas, where for the first time Palestinian police exchanged fire with Israeli soldiers. Israel deployed tanks and helicopters around Palestinian cities. Reported death tolls vary: the Palestinian Centre for Human Rights and Israeli and international press accounts put the dead at between 64 and 74 Palestinians and 15 and 17 Israeli soldiers, with more than 1,000 Palestinians and dozens of Israelis wounded. The Security Council called for a halt to violence, and President Clinton summoned Netanyahu and Arafat to Washington on 1-2 October to restart talks.

perspectives.framing: Netanyahu said the 'Hasmonean tunnel' exit was an archaeological and tourism project that did not affect the mosques, accused Arafat of incitement, and condemned Palestinian policemen who fired on Israeli soldiers.

Arafat called the opening a 'big crime against our religious and holy places' and an attempt to change Jerusalem's status, and defended Palestinian police as protecting demonstrators from Israeli fire.

The Security Council in Resolution 1073 called for the immediate cessation of all acts that had negative results on the peace process and for the safe return to normalcy; the Special Committee on Israeli practices recorded the casualty figures.

B'Tselem found that Israeli police used lethal force at the Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif in situations where their lives were not threatened; PCHR documented Palestinian deaths across the territories.

title: Hebron Protocol divides the city into H1 and H2
summary: On 17 January 1997 Israel and the PLO signed the Protocol Concerning the Redeployment in Hebron, the first agreement concluded by the Netanyahu government with the Palestinians, after months of US-mediated talks in which King Hussein of Jordan intervened. Netanyahu and Arafat had shaken hands on the deal at Erez on 14 January. The protocol, a supplement to the 1995 Interim Agreement, divided Hebron into area H1, about 80 percent of the city, transferred to Palestinian Authority civil and security control, and H2, containing the Israeli settler enclaves and the Cave of the Patriarchs / Ibrahimi Mosque, where Israel retained security responsibility. Israeli forces redeployed within days. An attached US 'Note for the Record' set out further Israeli redeployments and Palestinian obligations, and the Temporary International Presence in Hebron was re-established.

perspectives.framing: Netanyahu presented the protocol as proof that Likud would honour signed agreements while securing better protection for Hebron's Jewish community and the principle of reciprocity; settler leaders and some coalition members opposed it.
The PA welcomed the transfer of most of Hebron as overdue implementation of Oslo II, while objecting that Israeli control of H2 left tens of thousands of Palestinians under military rule.

The United States, through envoy Dennis Ross, framed the protocol and its Note for the Record as reviving the peace process and committing both sides to further redeployments and security cooperation.
Hamas dismissed the protocol as consolidating the settler presence in the heart of Hebron and continuing the fragmentation of Palestinian land.

location: White House, Washington, D.C. (negotiated at Wye River, Maryland)
title: Wye River Memorandum signed to revive Oslo implementation
summary: On 23 October 1998 Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Chairman Yasser Arafat signed the Wye River Memorandum at the White House after nine days of talks at the Wye River conference centre in Maryland led by President Bill Clinton, with King Hussein of Jordan present at the ceremony. The memorandum set out steps to resume implementation of the 1995 Interim Agreement: Israeli further redeployment from an additional 13 percent of the West Bank, transferring 1 percent to Area A and 12 percent to Area B (3 percent of it as nature reserves), and the shift of 14.2 percent from Area B to Area A; Palestinian security commitments, including a plan to combat armed groups verified with US assistance; reaffirmation of the annulment of hostile clauses in the Palestinian National Charter; and resumed permanent-status talks. Israel completed only the first phase before suspending implementation in December 1998.

perspectives.framing: Netanyahu portrayed Wye as securing reciprocity, concrete Palestinian security obligations verified by the CIA, and a limited land transfer, but coalition partners on the right accused him of surrendering territory.

The PA welcomed the resumption of redeployments as overdue Israeli compliance with Oslo II and framed the security clauses as commitments it was already fulfilling, while insisting on a state by May 1999.
The Clinton administration described the memorandum as breaking an 18-month deadlock and committed the CIA to verify security steps and the US to assist with economic and security needs.
Hamas rejected the memorandum as a security agreement that turned the Authority into an instrument for suppressing resistance, and Israel and the PA arrested its activists in its wake.

title: Israel withdraws from its southern Lebanon security zone
summary: On 24 May 2000 Israel completed a unilateral withdrawal of its forces from the self-declared security zone it had held in southern Lebanon since 1985, ending an 18-year military presence that began with the 1982 invasion. Prime Minister Ehud Barak had pledged to leave by July 2000 without waiting for a peace agreement with Syria and Lebanon. The withdrawal was accelerated when Israel's ally, the South Lebanon Army, collapsed over 22-24 May; Hezbollah fighters and villagers moved into the evacuated villages, thousands of SLA members and families fled into Israel, and detainees in Khiam prison were freed. The United Nations identified a line of withdrawal, the Blue Line, and on 16 June 2000 the Secretary-General reported that Israel had withdrawn in accordance with Security Council Resolution 425, a conclusion the Council endorsed on 18 June.

perspectives.framing: Barak presented the pullout as fulfilling an election promise, ending a costly deployment and removing any pretext for Hezbollah attacks, with UN certification giving Israel international legitimacy on the border.

Hezbollah celebrated 25 May as 'Resistance and Liberation Day', claiming the first Arab victory over Israel achieved by force, and asserted that the Shebaa Farms remained occupied, justifying continued resistance.
Lebanon welcomed the liberation of its territory but disputed the Blue Line at several points, including the Shebaa Farms, and declined to deploy the army to the border.

The Secretary-General and UNIFIL described the Blue Line as a line of withdrawal for the purpose of confirming compliance with Resolution 425, not an international border, and confirmed Israel's withdrawal on 16 June 2000.

title: Camp David summit on permanent status ends without agreement
summary: From 11 to 25 July 2000 President Bill Clinton hosted Prime Minister Ehud Barak and Chairman Yasser Arafat at Camp David for an intensive summit intended to reach a framework agreement on permanent status. The talks addressed borders and territory, settlements, Jerusalem, refugees and security. Accounts by participants and press reports indicate that Israel offered a Palestinian state on most of the West Bank and all of Gaza with partial arrangements in East Jerusalem, and that the sides could not agree on sovereignty over the Old City and the Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif or on the refugees' claimed right of return. On 25 July Clinton announced that no agreement had been reached; a trilateral statement committed the parties to continue negotiating and to avoid unilateral actions. Clinton publicly praised Barak's flexibility, and the failure preceded the outbreak of the second intifada two months later.

perspectives.framing: Barak said he had offered unprecedented concessions, including on Jerusalem, and that Arafat's refusal to make a counter-offer showed there was 'no partner' for peace, a narrative that shaped Israeli politics afterwards.

Palestinian negotiators argued the offer would have left a non-contiguous state without sovereignty over the Haram al-Sharif or a solution for refugees, that the summit was premature and poorly prepared, and that they were unfairly blamed.

Clinton's statement called the talks the most far-reaching ever held, credited Barak with moving further than Arafat, and urged both sides to keep negotiating; US aides later differed over the allocation of blame.
Hamas said the summit's collapse proved that negotiations could not achieve Palestinian rights and called for renewed resistance.

title: Sharon visits Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif; Second Intifada begins
summary: On 28 September 2000, Likud opposition leader Ariel Sharon toured the Temple Mount / Haram al-Sharif compound in Jerusalem's Old City, escorted by a large Israeli police contingent, to assert Israeli sovereignty over the site after the collapse of the Camp David summit. Palestinian demonstrators clashed with police during the visit, and on 29 September, after Friday prayers, Israeli police used live fire on stone-throwing crowds inside the compound; contemporaneous reports cited by PBS and The Times of Israel put the number of Palestinians killed that day in Jerusalem at up to seven. Protests and armed confrontations spread rapidly across the West Bank, Gaza Strip and, within days, Arab towns inside Israel. It is widely treated as the start of the Second, or Al-Aqsa, Intifada, an uprising lasting roughly until 2005 that, per Encyclopaedia Britannica, produced more than 4,300 deaths at a ratio of roughly three Palestinians to one Israeli.

perspectives.framing: Israeli officials described the visit as a legitimate tour by a member of the Knesset of the holiest site in Judaism and argued that the uprising was premeditated by the Palestinian leadership after the failure of Camp David, using the visit as a pretext; Israel refers to the compound as the Temple Mount and to the uprising as the 'Palestinian terror war' or 'Oslo war'.

Palestinian leaders called the visit a deliberate provocation at Al-Aqsa Mosque, the third-holiest site in Islam, and framed the ensuing 'Al-Aqsa Intifada' as a popular uprising against occupation and the failure of Oslo to deliver a state.

Security Council resolution 1322 of 7 October 2000 deplored the provocation carried out at Al-Haram al-Sharif and condemned the excessive use of force against Palestinians, while calling on Israel to abide by the Fourth Geneva Convention; the Mitchell Committee later found the visit did not cause the uprising but was poorly timed.

location: Umm al-Fahm and Galilee towns, Israel
title: October 2000 killings of Arab citizens of Israel; Or Commission
summary: Between 1 and 8 October 2000, protests by Palestinian citizens of Israel in Galilee and Triangle towns such as Umm al-Fahm, Nazareth and Sakhnin, held in solidarity with Palestinians in the occupied territories, turned into confrontations with Israeli police. Officers used live ammunition and rubber-coated bullets; per the legal centre Adalah, thirteen unarmed Palestinians were shot dead, twelve of them citizens of Israel and one a resident of Gaza, and hundreds were injured. The government of Ehud Barak appointed a state commission of inquiry under Supreme Court Justice Theodor Or on 8 November 2000. Its report, published on 1 September 2003, found that there had been no justification for the lethal fire, criticised senior police commanders and political leaders, and recommended reforms. No officer was indicted, a point that families and rights groups continue to raise, and the events deepened the estrangement between the state and its Arab minority.

perspectives.framing: The Barak government described the events as violent riots that blocked roads and endangered lives during a national emergency, appointed the Or Commission to examine police conduct, and later accepted its recommendations; Ehud Barak publicly apologised to the families in 2019.

perspectives.party: Arab citizens of Israel and human-rights organisations
perspectives.framing: Adalah and the High Follow-Up Committee call the events the 'October 2000 killings' or 'October uprising', describe the dead as unarmed demonstrators shot by police snipers, and cite the absence of any indictment as evidence of impunity.

title: Taba talks end without a permanent-status agreement
summary: From 21 to 27 January 2001, Israeli and Palestinian delegations met at the Egyptian Red Sea resort of Taba in a final attempt to reach a permanent-status agreement before Israel's 6 February election. Israel's team was led by Foreign Minister Shlomo Ben-Ami and included Yossi Beilin and Gilad Sher; the Palestinian team was headed by Ahmed Qurei and included Saeb Erekat, Nabil Shaath and Mohammed Dahlan. Negotiators worked from the parameters President Bill Clinton had presented in December 2000 and discussed territory, Jerusalem, refugees and security. Their joint statement of 27 January said the sides had never been closer to agreement but that time constraints made a deal impossible; EU envoy Miguel Moratinos later recorded the positions in an unofficial paper. Ariel Sharon won the election and did not resume the talks, ending the Oslo-era permanent-status process.

perspectives.framing: The Barak government's negotiators described Taba as evidence of Israel's far-reaching offers; the incoming Sharon government said the talks were held by a caretaker government without a mandate and declared their positions non-binding.

Palestinian negotiators said Taba showed that agreement on borders based on the 1967 lines, Jerusalem and refugees was within reach and argued that Israel's election, not Palestinian rejectionism, ended the process.
EU special envoy Miguel Moratinos compiled a 'non-paper' recording the positions reached, which the EU presented as proof of substantial progress on all core issues.

title: Dolphinarium discotheque suicide bombing in Tel Aviv
summary: On the night of 1 June 2001, a suicide bomber detonated explosives packed with ball bearings among a crowd of young people queuing outside the Dolphinarium discotheque on the Tel Aviv beachfront. According to the Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 21 Israelis were killed, most of them teenagers from families that had immigrated from the former Soviet Union, and dozens more were wounded; The Jerusalem Post put the number injured at 132. The bomber, Saeed Hotari from the Jenin area, was affiliated with Hamas, which claimed the attack. It was the deadliest single attack inside Israel since the intifada had begun eight months earlier. Under heavy international pressure, Yasser Arafat announced a unilateral ceasefire the following day and Israel's government held back from a large-scale military response, although the lull proved short-lived.

perspectives.framing: Israel called the bombing a 'massacre' of children by a Hamas terrorist, held the Palestinian Authority responsible for failing to act against armed groups, and cited it in demanding that Arafat arrest militants.
Hamas claimed the bombing as a 'martyrdom operation' by its military wing in retaliation for Israeli killings of Palestinians, framing attacks inside Israel as legitimate resistance to occupation.
Arafat condemned the attack and declared a ceasefire, presenting it as a Palestinian commitment to restore calm while accusing Israel of provoking violence through incursions and closures.

title: Sbarro pizzeria suicide bombing in central Jerusalem
summary: On 9 August 2001, at lunchtime, a suicide bomber detonated a device inside the Sbarro pizzeria at the corner of King George Street and Jaffa Road, one of the busiest intersections in central Jerusalem. According to the Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 15 people were killed, including seven children, and about 130 were wounded. Hamas and Palestinian Islamic Jihad both claimed responsibility; the bomber, Izz al-Din al-Masri from the Jenin area, had been guided to the site by Ahlam Tamimi, who was convicted in Israel, released in the 2011 Shalit exchange and later charged in the United States, where two victims held citizenship. Israel responded by seizing Orient House, the PLO's headquarters in East Jerusalem, and stepping up strikes on Palestinian Authority facilities, while the attack hardened international views of the escalating violence and increased pressure on Yasser Arafat to act against armed groups.

perspectives.framing: Israel described the bombing as a terrorist massacre targeting families and children, responded by closing Orient House and other PA institutions in Jerusalem, and cited the attack as proof that the PA was not preventing terrorism.

Hamas's military wing claimed the bombing as retaliation for Israel's targeted killings, including a strike in Nablus days earlier, and framed it as resistance; Tamimi has since described the attack without regret in interviews.
Washington condemned the attack, later listed Tamimi as a wanted terrorist and filed charges in 2017, while also criticising Israel's seizure of Orient House as an escalation.

title: Passover bombing at the Park Hotel, Netanya
summary: On the evening of 27 March 2002, as some 250 guests gathered for the Passover seder in the dining room of the Park Hotel in the coastal city of Netanya, a suicide bomber walked past hotel security and detonated a large explosive device. According to the Israel Ministry of Foreign Affairs, 30 people were killed, many of them elderly and including Holocaust survivors, and about 140 were wounded; early reports carried by CNN that night gave a toll of 19. Hamas claimed responsibility and identified the bomber as Abdel-Basset Odeh from Tulkarm. The attack was the deadliest against Israeli civilians of the Second Intifada and came at the end of a month of repeated bombings in Israeli cities. Two days later Israel's cabinet ordered Operation Defensive Shield, the largest West Bank military operation since 1967, and the timing overshadowed the Arab League summit in Beirut.

perspectives.framing: Israel called the attack the 'Passover massacre', a deliberate slaughter of civilians at a religious meal, declared the Palestinian Authority an entity that supports terrorism, and cited the bombing as the trigger for Operation Defensive Shield.
Hamas claimed the bombing as a 'martyrdom operation' by its Izz ad-Din al-Qassam Brigades and presented it as a response to Israeli military operations in the West Bank and Gaza.

The Secretary-General condemned the bombing as a terrorist attack on civilians and, within days, the Security Council adopted resolution 1402 calling for a ceasefire and Israeli withdrawal from Palestinian cities.

title: Arab League summit in Beirut adopts the Arab Peace Initiative
summary: On 28 March 2002, the 14th Arab League summit in Beirut unanimously adopted a peace proposal put forward by Saudi Crown Prince Abdullah. The Arab Peace Initiative offered Israel an end to the Arab-Israeli conflict, a peace agreement and normal relations with all Arab states in exchange for a full Israeli withdrawal from the territories occupied since June 1967, including the Syrian Golan Heights and remaining Lebanese territory, the establishment of an independent Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital in the West Bank and Gaza Strip, and a just solution to the Palestinian refugee question agreed in accordance with UN General Assembly resolution 194. The summit was overshadowed by the Park Hotel bombing the previous evening and by Yasser Arafat's absence after Israel restricted his travel. Israel's government did not accept the plan, though later Arab summits re-endorsed it and the Quartet's Road Map referenced it.

perspectives.framing: Arab states presented the initiative as a historic collective offer of comprehensive peace and normalisation on the basis of 'land for peace' and international legitimacy, and have repeatedly reaffirmed it as a package rather than a starting point for negotiation.

The Sharon government said the plan was a non-starter because it demanded withdrawal to the 1967 lines and a refugee solution based on resolution 194 before negotiations; later Israeli leaders described elements as positive while rejecting its terms as preconditions.
The PLO endorsed the initiative as the Arab consensus for a two-state settlement on the 1967 lines and has cited it in every subsequent negotiation as the framework for a regional peace.

title: Operation Defensive Shield and the battle of Jenin refugee camp
summary: On 29 March 2002, two days after the Park Hotel bombing, Israel launched Operation Defensive Shield, its largest military operation in the West Bank since 1967. Over the following weeks the IDF entered Ramallah, where Yasser Arafat's Muqata compound was besieged, and Tulkarm, Qalqilya, Bethlehem, Jenin and Nablus, imposing curfews and mass arrests. The most contested fighting took place in the Jenin refugee camp from 3 April, where troops faced booby-trapped alleys and armed groups. The UN Secretary-General's report to the General Assembly (A/ES-10/186, August 2002) found that at least 52 Palestinians, up to half of them possibly civilians, and 23 Israeli soldiers died there, did not substantiate early Palestinian claims of a massacre of hundreds, and documented extensive destruction of the camp. Human Rights Watch counted at least 52 Palestinian dead, including 22 civilians. The Church of the Nativity siege in Bethlehem ended on 10 May 2002.

perspectives.framing: Israel described the operation as a defensive campaign to dismantle the 'terrorist infrastructure' behind the suicide bombings, said Jenin camp was a base for attackers, and rejected massacre allegations as a libel, pointing out that it sent infantry rather than bombing the camp from the air.

Palestinian officials called the operation a reoccupation of Area A in violation of Oslo, described the siege of Arafat as an attempt to topple him, and initially alleged that hundreds had been killed in Jenin, later citing the camp's destruction as a war crime.

Security Council resolutions 1402 and 1403 demanded Israeli withdrawal; a proposed fact-finding team was disbanded after Israel objected, and the Secretary-General's report relied on secondary sources, calling for accountability while giving no support to the massacre claim.

Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International documented unlawful killings, use of civilians as human shields and disproportionate destruction in Jenin and Nablus and called for war-crimes investigations, while also condemning Palestinian bombings of Israeli civilians.

title: Israel approves and begins building the West Bank barrier
summary: In June 2002, at the height of the suicide-bombing campaign, Israel's cabinet approved and began building a physical barrier between Israel and the West Bank. The 23 June 2002 decision authorised a first phase running roughly 123 kilometres from the Salem checkpoint near Jenin south to the settlement of Elkana, plus sections north and south of Jerusalem; per UN OCHA, that stage was declared complete in July 2003. Rather than following the 1949 Green Line, the route, later planned at more than 700 kilometres of fences, walls, trenches and patrol roads, looped east to enclose settlements, placing Palestinian villages, farmland and East Jerusalem neighbourhoods on the Israeli side; per OCHA, some 85 percent of the planned route lies inside the West Bank. Israel's government described the barrier as a temporary security measure, while Palestinians and rights groups said it amounted to de facto annexation.

perspectives.framing: Israel calls the barrier the 'security fence' or 'anti-terror fence', a reversible, non-political defensive measure to stop infiltration from Judea and Samaria, and credits it with the sharp fall in suicide bombings after 2003.

Palestinians call it the 'separation wall' or 'apartheid wall', argue that its route inside the West Bank seizes land and water, isolates East Jerusalem and predetermines borders, and sought the ICJ advisory opinion through the UN General Assembly.

B'Tselem, Human Rights Watch and OCHA describe the barrier's humanitarian impact on access to land, services and family life and argue that a route on the Green Line would meet security needs without violating international law.

title: Quartet presents the Road Map for Peace
summary: On 30 April 2003, the Quartet of the United States, European Union, United Nations and Russia formally presented Israel and the Palestinian Authority with 'A Performance-Based Roadmap to a Permanent Two-State Solution'. The document set out three phases: an end to violence, Palestinian institutional reform and an Israeli settlement freeze and withdrawal from areas occupied since September 2000; an interim Palestinian state with provisional borders; and permanent-status negotiations aimed at a final settlement, originally targeted for 2005. Its release followed the appointment of Mahmoud Abbas as the first Palestinian prime minister, a condition pressed by Washington. Israel's cabinet accepted the plan on 25 May 2003 while attaching fourteen reservations, and Prime Ministers Ariel Sharon and Abbas endorsed it with President George W. Bush at Aqaba, Jordan, on 4 June 2003. Implementation stalled within months amid renewed attacks, military operations and Abbas's resignation in September.

perspectives.framing: The Bush administration presented the Road Map as the path to its June 2002 vision of two states, insisting on Palestinian security performance and reform as the first step and on reciprocal Israeli obligations on settlements.

Israel accepted 'the steps set out in the Road Map' subject to fourteen reservations, chiefly that Palestinian action against terrorism precede any Israeli obligation, that the refugee 'right of return' be excluded, and that the Arab Peace Initiative not be a reference.
The PA accepted the plan without reservations, stressed the settlement freeze and the 2005 statehood target, and argued that Israel's reservations and continued incursions emptied it of content.
Security Council resolution 1515 of 19 November 2003 endorsed the Road Map and called on the parties to fulfil their obligations under it.
