title: UN Security Council adopts Resolution 2728 demanding a ceasefire
summary: On 25 March 2024 the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2728 by 14 votes to none, with the United States abstaining, after three earlier ceasefire drafts had been vetoed by the United States or by Russia and China. The resolution demanded an immediate ceasefire for the month of Ramadan leading to a lasting and sustainable ceasefire, the immediate and unconditional release of all hostages, and the lifting of barriers to humanitarian assistance at scale. It was the Council's first ceasefire demand of the war, following resolutions 2712 and 2720 on humanitarian pauses and aid. The US abstention marked a public rift with Israel, whose prime minister cancelled a planned delegation to Washington in protest. Fighting continued and the parties disagreed over whether the resolution was binding; the Gaza Health Ministry's toll passed 32,000 that week.

perspectives.framing: The Secretary-General said the resolution must be implemented and that failure would be unforgivable; most Council members and the UN Secretariat treated it as binding on the parties.
Called the resolution a retreat from linking a ceasefire to the release of hostages, said it gave Hamas hope and vowed to continue operations until Hamas was defeated.
Welcomed the demand for a ceasefire, said it was ready for an immediate exchange of prisoners and hostages and accused Israel of defying the Council.

Explained its abstention by saying it supported the goals but objected to the absence of a condemnation of Hamas, and characterised the resolution as non-binding, a position contested by other members.

title: Israeli strike destroys Iranian consulate annex in Damascus
summary: On 1 April 2024 an air strike widely attributed to Israel destroyed a consular annex beside the Iranian embassy in the Mezzeh district of Damascus. Iran said seven members of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps were killed, including Brigadier General Mohammad Reza Zahedi, the senior Quds Force commander for Syria and Lebanon, and his deputy Mohammad Hadi Haji Rahimi; the Syrian Observatory for Human Rights counted 11 dead, including two Syrians and one Lebanese. Israel did not officially claim the strike, but Israeli officials said Zahedi was a legitimate military target directing attacks on Israel. Iran declared the building diplomatic premises and promised retaliation 'at the same magnitude', and on 13-14 April launched its first direct attack on Israeli territory. The strike was the most consequential of a long series of Israeli attacks on Iranian and Hezbollah targets in Syria since the Gaza war began.

perspectives.framing: Condemned the strike as an attack on sovereign diplomatic premises in violation of the Vienna Convention and a 'cowardly crime' by the 'Zionist regime', and reserved the right to respond.
Israeli officials said the building was a military facility used by the Quds Force, not a consulate, and that Zahedi was planning attacks on Israel; Israel maintained ambiguity about responsibility.
Said it had no involvement or advance notice, warned Iran against escalation and moved to reinforce regional air defences.
Denounced the strike as Israeli aggression on Syrian territory and called for international condemnation.

title: Israeli drone strikes kill seven World Central Kitchen aid workers
summary: On the night of 1 April 2024 three successive Israeli drone strikes hit a three-car convoy of the charity World Central Kitchen as it left a warehouse in Deir al-Balah after unloading food delivered by sea, killing seven aid workers: citizens of Australia, Poland and the United Kingdom, a US-Canadian dual national and a Palestinian driver. The vehicles were marked with the charity's logo and their movements had been coordinated with the IDF. On 5 April the IDF said the strikes were a grave mistake caused by misidentification of a suspected gunman and violations of its rules of engagement; it dismissed two officers and reprimanded three others. World Central Kitchen suspended operations in Gaza and demanded an independent inquiry. The killings prompted President Biden to press Israel on civilian protection, after which Israel announced the reopening of the Erez crossing and the port of Ashdod for aid.

perspectives.framing: Acknowledged a serious error by forces who wrongly believed a Hamas gunman was in the convoy, apologised, and pointed to disciplinary action as evidence of accountability.
Founder Jose Andres said the convoy was targeted 'systematically, car by car' despite coordination; Australia, Poland and the UK demanded full accountability and transparent investigations.
Cited the strikes as proof of deliberate targeting of aid operations and of a strategy of starvation.
President Biden said he was outraged, told Netanyahu that US support depended on concrete steps to protect civilians and aid workers, and pressed for an immediate ceasefire deal.

title: Iran attacks Israel directly; Israel strikes near Isfahan
summary: On the night of 13-14 April 2024 Iran launched what it called Operation True Promise, its first direct attack on Israeli territory, in retaliation for the Damascus consulate strike. According to the IDF, about 170 drones, more than 30 cruise missiles and more than 120 ballistic missiles were fired from Iran, with additional launches by the Houthis and Iraqi groups; Israel, the United States, Britain, France and Jordan intercepted about 99 per cent. A few ballistic missiles struck Nevatim airbase, causing light damage, and a seven-year-old Bedouin girl was seriously injured by falling shrapnel. Iran said the matter could be 'deemed concluded'. On 19 April an Israeli strike hit an air-defence radar near Isfahan, close to nuclear facilities, which Israel did not officially acknowledge and Iran played down. Both sides then stepped back from further direct exchanges until October 2024.

perspectives.framing: Framed the attack as a lawful exercise of self-defence under Article 51 of the UN Charter for the attack on its consulate, described it as calibrated and successful, and warned of a stronger response to any further Israeli action.

Called it an unprecedented act of aggression by the Iranian regime, credited a 'coalition' defence for foiling it, and said Israel would respond at a time of its choosing while showing restraint under US pressure.
Helped shoot down drones and missiles, urged Israel to 'take the win' and avoid a wider war, and coordinated new sanctions on Iran with the G7.
Said it intercepted objects violating its airspace to protect its citizens and denied acting in Israel's defence, while warning against regional escalation.

title: Rafah offensive; Israel seizes crossing and Philadelphi corridor
summary: On 6 May 2024 the IDF ordered about 100,000 people to leave eastern Rafah, where more than a million displaced Gazans had gathered, hours after Hamas announced it accepted a ceasefire proposal that Israel said differed from the one it had endorsed. On 7 May Israeli tanks seized the Palestinian side of the Rafah crossing with Egypt, which has remained closed to normal traffic since, and troops advanced into the city over the following weeks despite US warnings. On 29 May the IDF announced operational control of the entire 14-kilometre Philadelphi corridor along the Egyptian border, where it said it had found about 20 tunnels. UNRWA said on 28 May that around one million people had fled Rafah in three weeks, mostly to al-Mawasi and Khan Younis, and aid entry through the south fell sharply. Ceasefire negotiations stalled over the corridor's future.

perspectives.framing: Calls Rafah Hamas's last stronghold, the location of four remaining battalions and of smuggling tunnels into Egypt, and holds that control of the Philadelphi corridor is essential to prevent Hamas rearming.
Describes the offensive as an assault on a city of refugees, blames Israel for sabotaging the ceasefire it had accepted, and demands a full Israeli withdrawal including from the corridor.

Objected that Israel's seizure of the crossing and corridor violated the 1979 peace treaty's security annex and the 2005 crossing arrangements, refused to coordinate aid through an Israeli-held crossing and later joined the ICJ case.
Opposed a major operation in Rafah without a credible plan to protect civilians, paused a shipment of heavy bombs, then judged the operation more limited than it had feared.

title: ICC prosecutor seeks warrants; ICJ orders halt to Rafah offensive
summary: On 20 May 2024 ICC Prosecutor Karim Khan applied for arrest warrants for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Defence Minister Yoav Gallant on charges including starvation of civilians as a method of warfare, and for Hamas leaders Yahya Sinwar, Mohammed Deif and Ismail Haniyeh for extermination, murder, hostage-taking and sexual violence. Four days later the International Court of Justice, by 13 votes to 2, ordered Israel to immediately halt its military offensive and any other action in Rafah Governorate that could inflict on the Palestinian group in Gaza conditions of life that could bring about its physical destruction, to keep the Rafah crossing open for aid and to admit UN investigators. Israel said the order did not prohibit all operations in Rafah and continued fighting; the ICC judges issued warrants for Netanyahu, Gallant and Deif in November 2024.

perspectives.framing: Denounced the ICC application as a 'moral outrage' that equated a democracy with a 'terrorist' organisation, argued the ICC lacks jurisdiction, and read the ICJ order as permitting operations that do not create conditions of physical destruction.
Rejected the equating of 'victim and executioner' in the ICC application while welcoming the ICJ order as a demand for Israel to end its 'genocide' in Rafah.
The prosecutor said the applications followed an independent investigation and that no one is above the law; the court frames its role as impartial application of the Rome Statute.

President Biden called the ICC application outrageous and rejected any equivalence between Israel and Hamas; Washington said it did not believe Israel's Rafah operation amounted to a major ground offensive.
Called the ICJ order a clear, unambiguous instruction to stop the Rafah assault and urged enforcement through the Security Council.

title: Strike and fire at displaced persons' camp in Tel al-Sultan, Rafah
summary: On the night of 26 May 2024, two days after the ICJ order on Rafah, an Israeli air strike on the Tel al-Sultan area of northwestern Rafah set off a fire that swept through a camp of tents and shelters for displaced people near a UNRWA logistics base. The Gaza Health Ministry said 45 people were killed and more than 200 injured. The IDF said it had targeted and killed two senior Hamas officials, Yassin Rabia and Khaled Nagar, with two small precision munitions, that the site lay outside the designated humanitarian zone, and that the fire was probably caused by a secondary blast of fuel or weapons stored nearby, a claim it said was under investigation. Prime Minister Netanyahu called the deaths a 'tragic mishap'. Images of the burning camp prompted international condemnation, statements by UN human-rights experts and a UN Security Council emergency meeting.

perspectives.framing: Says the strike was precise, lawful and aimed at senior Hamas commanders, that it did not expect civilian harm and that the fire's cause was under review; it disputes descriptions of a deliberate attack on a safe zone.
Calls the attack a massacre of displaced civilians in a 'safe zone' and defiance of the ICJ, and demands international sanctions on Israel.

The Secretary-General said there was 'no safe place in Gaza' and that the horror must stop, UNRWA described the camp as sheltering civilians who had followed evacuation orders, and OHCHR called for a full investigation.
Foreign-policy chief Josep Borrell said the strike was horrifying and called for the ICJ order to be respected; France and others urged an immediate ceasefire.

title: Israeli raid rescues four hostages in Nuseirat
summary: On 8 June 2024 Israeli special forces, in a daytime operation the IDF codenamed 'Arnon', rescued four hostages, Noa Argamani, Almog Meir Jan, Andrey Kozlov and Shlomi Ziv, from two apartment buildings in the crowded Nuseirat refugee camp where they had been held since 7 October. The raid was supported by intense air and artillery strikes covering the extraction, and one police counter-terrorism officer, Arnon Zamora, was killed. The Gaza Health Ministry said 274 Palestinians were killed and 698 injured in the camp and nearby areas; the IDF said it knew of fewer than 100 casualties, including militants who fired on its forces. It was the largest single hostage rescue of the war and was celebrated in Israel, while the scale of Palestinian deaths drew condemnation from the UN and criticism from human-rights groups over the use of force in a densely populated area.

perspectives.framing: Presents the rescue as a heroic and lawful operation that proved hostages were being held in civilian homes by Hamas, and attributes civilian casualties to Hamas fighters engaging troops from within the camp.
Calls the raid the 'Nuseirat massacre', accuses Israel of killing hundreds of civilians to free four captives and says some hostages were killed by Israeli fire during the operation.
The human rights office said the deaths and injuries raised serious concern about compliance with the principles of distinction, proportionality and precaution, and called for an investigation.
Welcomed the rescue and said it had provided intelligence support, while reiterating that a ceasefire deal was the only way to free all hostages.

title: ICJ advisory opinion finds Israel's occupation unlawful
summary: On 19 July 2024 the International Court of Justice delivered an advisory opinion requested by the UN General Assembly in December 2022 on the legal consequences of Israel's policies and practices in the occupied Palestinian territory. By 11 votes to 4 the court found that Israel's continued presence in the West Bank, East Jerusalem and Gaza is unlawful and that Israel must end it as rapidly as possible; by 14 votes to 1 it held that Israel must cease settlement activity, evacuate settlers and make reparation, and that other states must not recognise or assist the situation. It also found that Israel's policies breached the prohibition of racial segregation and apartheid under Article 3 of the CERD convention, without adjudicating which term applied. Although non-binding, it was the court's most sweeping statement on the occupation; the General Assembly in September 2024 demanded that Israel end its presence within twelve months.

perspectives.framing: Rejected the opinion as one-sided, 'a decision of lies' that ignored Israel's security needs and the 7 October attack, and asserted that the Jewish people are not occupiers in their own land, using the term Judea and Samaria for the West Bank.
Hailed a historic ruling confirming that the occupation and settlements are illegal and demanded that states impose sanctions and end arms sales to Israel.

The Secretary-General transmitted the opinion to the General Assembly, which endorsed it; UN officials described the finding as consistent with long-standing UN positions on the illegality of settlements.

Said it was concerned by the breadth of the opinion, argued it would complicate efforts toward a negotiated two-state solution and rejected the idea that the court could compel a unilateral withdrawal.

title: Majdal Shams strike; Fuad Shukr and Ismail Haniyeh killed
summary: On 27 July 2024 a rocket struck a football pitch in the Druze town of Majdal Shams in the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights, killing 12 children and teenagers, the deadliest attack on Israeli-held territory since 7 October. Israel and the United States said it was a Hezbollah Falaq-1 rocket; Hezbollah denied responsibility. On 30 July an Israeli strike on an apartment building in Haret Hreik in Beirut's southern suburbs killed Fuad Shukr, Hezbollah's most senior military commander, and, according to Lebanese officials, several civilians including children. Hours later, in the early hours of 31 July, Hamas political chief Ismail Haniyeh was killed by an explosion at a guesthouse in Tehran after attending President Pezeshkian's inauguration; Iran and Hamas blamed Israel, which did not comment at the time. Iran and Hezbollah vowed revenge, and Hezbollah launched a large barrage on 25 August after Israeli pre-emptive strikes.

perspectives.framing: Held Hezbollah responsible for a massacre of children and described the killing of Shukr as the response; it maintained ambiguity on Haniyeh while officials said all Hamas leaders were legitimate targets.
Denied firing at Majdal Shams, suggesting an Israeli interceptor was responsible, mourned Shukr as a 'great commander' and promised a definite response to the Beirut strike.
Called Haniyeh's killing a violation of its sovereignty and a 'cowardly' assassination by the 'Zionist regime', and Supreme Leader Khamenei said Israel would face harsh punishment.
Mourned Haniyeh as a 'martyr' and said the assassination would not go unanswered, while continuing ceasefire talks under Yahya Sinwar, who was named as his successor.
Backed Israel's attribution of the Majdal Shams strike to Hezbollah, urged restraint on all sides and said it had no advance knowledge of the Tehran operation.

title: Gaza Health Ministry death toll passes 40,000
summary: On 15 August 2024 the Gaza Health Ministry reported that 40,005 Palestinians had been killed and 92,401 injured since 7 October 2023, a figure that UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk cited while stressing that thousands more were believed buried under rubble. The ministry's tally does not distinguish combatants from civilians; it said most of the identified dead were women and children. Israel disputes the composition of the toll: the IDF said by that month that it had killed some 17,000 Hamas and other militants, and Israeli officials questioned the ministry's methods, although Israeli intelligence assessments cited by the press regarded the overall figure as broadly reliable. Independent studies published in The Lancet argued the true number of direct and indirect deaths was likely higher. The IDF reported more than 300 of its soldiers killed in Gaza since the ground invasion began.

perspectives.framing: Presents the toll as a count of 'martyrs' compiled from hospital records and verified family reports, most of them civilians, and says the real total is higher because of the missing.

Argues that Hamas controls the ministry and inflates or misclassifies deaths, that a large share of the dead are combatants, and that the civilian-to-combatant ratio is lower than in comparable urban wars.

OHCHR High Commissioner Volker Turk called the 40,000 figure a grim milestone and urged an end to the fighting; UN agencies use the ministry's numbers, which they have found credible in past conflicts, while noting they cannot independently verify them.

Studies in The Lancet found the ministry's data internally consistent and suggested that direct deaths were under-recorded and that indirect deaths from disease and hunger would raise the total substantially.

title: Humanitarian pauses agreed for Gaza polio vaccination campaign
summary: On 29 August 2024 the World Health Organization announced that Israel had agreed to a series of localised humanitarian pauses to allow a mass polio vaccination campaign in Gaza, after the first confirmed case of poliovirus in the territory in 25 years, a ten-month-old child in Deir al-Balah, was reported in August and the virus had been detected in wastewater in July. The plan, negotiated by WHO and UNICEF with COGAT, the Israeli military coordination body, and accepted by Hamas, provided three-day pauses in fighting from 6 am to 3 pm in central, southern and then northern Gaza in turn, beginning on 1 September. The campaign aimed to reach more than 640,000 children under ten with two doses of novel oral polio vaccine; the first round, run from 1 to 12 September, reached about 560,000 children. It was the first agreed pause in fighting since the November 2023 truce.

perspectives.framing: WHO and UNICEF described the pauses as a narrow humanitarian necessity, not a ceasefire, and warned that polio's return reflected the collapse of water and sanitation in Gaza.
COGAT said it coordinated the campaign and the entry of vaccines as part of its humanitarian efforts, while insisting that operations against Hamas would continue outside the agreed windows.
Said it would cooperate with the campaign and called for a full ceasefire, blaming Israel's destruction of infrastructure for the outbreak.
Welcomed the arrangement and pressed both parties to observe the pauses and to reach a broader ceasefire deal.

title: Six hostages found killed in a Rafah tunnel; mass protests and strike in Israel
summary: On 1 September 2024 the Israel Defense Forces announced that troops had recovered the bodies of six hostages, Hersh Goldberg-Polin, Carmel Gat, Eden Yerushalmi, Alexander Lobanov, Almog Sarusi and Ori Danino, from a tunnel beneath Rafah in southern Gaza, about a kilometre from where hostage Farhan al-Qadi had been rescued alive days earlier. The IDF said they had been shot by their captors shortly before soldiers reached them; Hamas blamed Israel for refusing a ceasefire. Large protests followed across Israel, and the Histadrut labour federation called a general strike on 2 September that a Tel Aviv labour court ordered ended that afternoon as 'political'. Gaza's health ministry counted 40,861 Palestinians killed since October 2023 as of 4 September, per IRNA; Israel publishes no cumulative total, but the IDF had claimed about 17,000 Hamas fighters killed as of July 2024, later lowered to about 15,000, according to The Jerusalem Post.

perspectives.framing: Described the six as 'brutally murdered by Hamas terrorists' shortly before rescue, said whoever murders hostages does not want a deal, and vowed to bring those responsible to justice while insisting the government remained committed to an agreement that protects Israel's security.

Blamed Israel for the deaths, saying its refusal to sign a ceasefire and its military pressure in Rafah caused the hostages to be killed, and framed the captives as 'prisoners' held in the 'resistance's' custody.

perspectives.party: Hostage families and Israeli protest movement
perspectives.framing: Accused Prime Minister Netanyahu of abandoning the hostages and prioritising political survival over a deal, and called a nationwide strike to 'bring the nation to a halt'.
The Secretary-General 'utterly condemned' the killing of the six hostages and reiterated his call for the immediate release of all hostages and an immediate ceasefire.

title: Pager and radio explosions strike Hezbollah members across Lebanon
summary: On the afternoon of 17 September 2024 thousands of pagers carried by Hezbollah members exploded almost simultaneously across Lebanon after receiving a message; a second wave of exploding hand-held radios followed on 18 September, some at funerals. Lebanon's health minister said the first wave killed at least nine people and wounded about 2,800, at least 200 of them seriously, most with injuries to the face, hands and midsection, according to CNN and NPR. The second wave killed at least 20 and injured more than 450, per the health ministry cited by VOA, a toll the minister later raised to 25. Hezbollah and the Lebanese government blamed Israel, which did not comment at the time. Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International said the devices also harmed civilians and called for an international investigation. The attacks preceded Israel's intensified air campaign across Lebanon from 23 September.

perspectives.framing: Called the explosions an Israeli 'aggression' and 'massacre' against its members and Lebanese civilians, vowed punishment, and said it would continue what it calls its support front for Gaza.

Condemned the blasts as a criminal attack on Lebanese sovereignty, emphasised civilian and health-worker casualties reported by its health ministry, and later lodged a complaint with the International Labour Organization.
Made no official comment at the time; Israeli officials and former intelligence officers later portrayed the operation as a precise blow against Hezbollah's communications network and combatants.

The Special Coordinator for the Middle East expressed grave concern at the risk of wide-scale regional escalation and urged all sides to de-escalate; UN human rights officials questioned the legality of detonating devices without knowing who held them.

title: Israeli airstrike kills Hezbollah leader Hassan Nasrallah in Beirut
summary: On the evening of 27 September 2024 Israeli aircraft dropped bunker-busting bombs on what Israel described as Hezbollah's central headquarters, built beneath residential buildings in Haret Hreik in Beirut's southern suburbs (Dahiyeh), levelling several apartment blocks in the largest blasts to hit the capital since October 2023. On 28 September Israel announced that Hassan Nasrallah, Hezbollah's leader for more than three decades, had been killed together with Ali Karki, commander of its southern front, and other commanders; Hezbollah confirmed his death the same day. Lebanon's health ministry gave a preliminary toll of two killed and 76 wounded, then six killed and 91 wounded; by the next day it counted 33 killed and 195 injured, a figure that also covered overnight strikes on the suburbs, according to Carnegie's Diwan. Iran vowed the killing would be avenged; Israel presented it as a decisive blow against Hezbollah.

perspectives.framing: Called the strike a targeted 'elimination' of the man responsible for decades of attacks on Israelis, a historic turning point that dismantled Hezbollah's command, and said it acted in self-defence to return displaced residents to northern Israel.
Mourned Nasrallah as a 'martyr' killed in a 'treacherous Zionist' strike on civilian buildings, pledged to continue fighting, and framed his death as part of its 'resistance' in support of Gaza.

Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei called Nasrallah 'a path and a school of thought', declared national mourning, and said his blood would not go unavenged, later citing the killing among the reasons for its 1 October missile attack.

The Secretary-General voiced deep concern at the humanitarian consequences in Lebanon, repeated his call for a cessation of hostilities and full implementation of resolution 1701, and noted UNIFIL peacekeepers remained in position.

title: Iran fires ballistic missile barrage at Israel
summary: On the evening of 1 October 2024 Iran launched about 180 ballistic missiles at Israel in at least two waves, its largest attack of the conflict, which Tehran called retaliation for the killings of Ismail Haniyeh, Hassan Nasrallah and Revolutionary Guard general Abbas Nilforoushan. The Israel Defense Forces estimated 180 projectiles (The Times of Israel counted 181) and said most were intercepted with US help, although some struck the ground, including at Nevatim air base in the Negev, damaging a hangar and taxiway. Iran claimed 90 per cent of its missiles hit their targets. One Palestinian man was killed and several people injured by falling debris in Jericho, in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, and two Israelis were lightly hurt in Tel Aviv. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu said Iran had made a 'big mistake' and 'will pay for it'; Israel struck Iranian military sites on 26 October.

perspectives.framing: Its UN mission called the barrage a lawful response to 'the terrorist acts of the Zionist regime', including the killings of Haniyeh in Tehran and Nasrallah in Beirut, and said it would cease unless Israel escalated further.

Described the attack as a grave act of aggression that failed thanks to air defences and US support, said Iran had made a 'big mistake' and would pay, and cast the episode as part of a war against Iran's 'axis'.
Condemned the attack, said US destroyers helped intercept missiles, and reaffirmed an 'ironclad' commitment to Israel's security while urging restraint to avoid a wider war.
The Secretary-General strongly condemned the 'massive missile attack by Iran on Israel', as he had in April, and called on all parties to step back from a widening regional conflict.

title: Israel launches ground incursion into southern Lebanon
summary: On 1 October 2024, after a week of intensified air strikes across Lebanon and the killing of Hassan Nasrallah, Israeli ground forces crossed into southern Lebanon in what the Israel Defense Forces called 'limited, localized, and targeted ground raids' against Hezbollah targets and infrastructure. Paratroopers, commandos and armoured units took part; Israel told the United States the operation would be limited in scope, scale and duration, while the White House warned of 'mission creep'. The stated aim was to remove 'immediate threats' from border villages, including Hezbollah's ability to infiltrate northern Israel. Hezbollah kept up rocket and drone fire, and fighting continued until the 27 November ceasefire. By 25 November Lebanon's health ministry counted 3,768 killed and 15,699 injured since 8 October 2023, per UN OCHA; Human Rights Watch, citing the ministry, put the toll through the ceasefire at more than 3,961 killed, including 736 women and 248 children.

perspectives.framing: Described the operation as limited, targeted raids against Hezbollah positions and tunnels threatening the border, part of a war of self-defence whose stated goal was the safe return of about 60,000 displaced residents of northern Israel.
Called the incursion an invasion, claimed to have repelled Israeli units in 'face-to-face' combat, and presented its continued rocket fire as resistance in support of Gaza and defence of Lebanon.

Condemned the invasion as a violation of Lebanese sovereignty, highlighted the mass displacement and death toll recorded by its health ministry, and appealed for a ceasefire and implementation of resolution 1701.

The Secretary-General said an all-out war in Lebanon must be avoided at all costs, that Lebanon's territorial integrity must be respected, and that civilians were paying a terrible price; UNIFIL refused Israeli requests to relocate its positions.

title: Israeli troops kill Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar in Rafah
summary: On 16 October 2024 soldiers of the Israel Defense Forces' 828th Bislamach Brigade on a routine patrol in Tel al-Sultan, Rafah, in the southern Gaza Strip, killed Hamas leader Yahya Sinwar, whom Israel called the mastermind of the 7 October 2023 attack. According to the IDF, a drone spotted three militants leaving a building and troops opened fire, unaware who they were; Sinwar entered a nearby building alone, a tank fired on it and he was found dead after throwing grenades at advancing troops. His identity was confirmed by DNA, fingerprint and dental tests. Israel said the war would continue; Hamas issued a defiant message. Gaza's health ministry counted at least 42,500 Palestinians killed since October 2023 as of 19 October, per CNN; Israel publishes no cumulative total, but the IDF claimed about 17,000 Hamas fighters killed as of July 2024, later lowered to about 15,000 (The Jerusalem Post).

perspectives.framing: Presented the killing as the 'elimination' of the architect of the 7 October massacre and a major step toward victory, urging Hamas fighters to lay down arms and release hostages, while saying the war would continue until Hamas was destroyed.

Mourned Sinwar as a 'martyr' who died fighting on the front line rather than hiding, said his death would strengthen the 'resistance', and insisted hostages would not be freed without an end to the war and Israeli withdrawal.
President Biden called it a good day for Israel, the United States and the world, said justice had been served, and argued the moment should be used to secure a hostage deal and end the war.

The Secretary-General did not comment on the killing itself but said it should lead to an immediate ceasefire, the unconditional release of all hostages and unrestricted humanitarian access; the Special Coordinator called it a critical juncture to 'silence the guns'.

title: Israeli air strikes on military sites in Iran
summary: In the early hours of 26 October 2024 dozens of Israeli aircraft, including fighter jets, refuelling and surveillance planes, struck targets in Iran that Israel said were missile and drone manufacturing sites and air-defence systems, in retaliation for Iran's 1 October missile barrage. Iran's army initially reported two soldiers killed and later said four soldiers and a civilian had died, two of the soldiers succumbing to wounds sustained defending Iranian airspace, according to IRNA and Gulf News. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei said Israel had 'made an error of calculation' and that the strikes 'should neither be downplayed nor exaggerated', leaving officials to weigh a response; in early November he threatened a 'crushing response' to Israel and the United States. Washington urged an end to the exchange of missile strikes. The operation was the first openly acknowledged Israeli air attack on Iranian territory.

perspectives.framing: Said the strikes were a proportionate, precise response to Iran's aggression that degraded missile production and air defences, demonstrated Israel's readiness to defend itself, and warned Iran that further escalation would bring a further response.

Played down the damage, said its air defences had countered most of the attack, asserted a right and duty to defend itself while noting its 'responsibilities towards regional peace', and lodged a complaint with the Security Council.
Described the Israeli action as an exercise of self-defence that avoided nuclear and oil facilities, and urged Iran not to respond so that the exchange could end.
The Secretary-General said all acts of escalation were condemnable and must stop, appealing to all parties to cease military action and return to diplomacy.

title: Knesset passes laws banning UNRWA activity in Israel
summary: On 28 October 2024 Israel's parliament, the Knesset, passed two laws targeting the UN Relief and Works Agency for Palestine Refugees (UNRWA): one barring the agency from operating in Israeli sovereign territory, approved by 92 votes to 10, and another prohibiting Israeli state bodies from any contact with UNRWA and revoking the 1967 arrangement under which it operates in areas under Israeli control, approved by 87 votes to 9, according to The Times of Israel and CNN. Both were to take effect after 90 days, on 30 January 2025. Israel accused UNRWA of infiltration by Hamas and of employing staff who took part in the 7 October attack. UN Secretary-General António Guterres said the laws, if implemented, would likely prevent UNRWA from continuing its essential work in the occupied Palestinian territory with devastating consequences for Palestine refugees, and that there was 'no alternative to UNRWA'.

perspectives.framing: Argued that UNRWA is compromised by Hamas, that some of its employees took part in the 7 October attack, and that the agency perpetuates the refugee issue; said other UN and aid bodies could deliver assistance instead.

The Secretary-General said there is no alternative to UNRWA, which is mandated by the General Assembly and is the principal channel for assistance to Palestine refugees; UNRWA called the laws collective punishment of refugees and noted that over 230 of its staff had been killed in Gaza.
Condemned the legislation as an attack on the rights of refugees and on the UN, and called on states to defend UNRWA's mandate and funding.
Expressed deep concern, urged Israel not to implement the laws, and stressed UNRWA's irreplaceable role in Gaza's humanitarian response.

title: ICC issues arrest warrants for Netanyahu, Gallant and Deif
summary: On 21 November 2024 Pre-Trial Chamber I of the International Criminal Court in The Hague rejected Israel's challenges to its jurisdiction and issued arrest warrants for Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, former defence minister Yoav Gallant and Mohammed Diab Ibrahim al-Masri ('Deif'), commander of Hamas's Qassam Brigades, whom Israel said it had killed in July. The judges found reasonable grounds to believe Netanyahu and Gallant bore responsibility for the war crimes of starvation as a method of warfare and intentionally attacking civilians, and for the crimes against humanity of murder, persecution and other inhumane acts, between 8 October 2023 and 20 May 2024; Deif's warrant covered murder, torture, rape, hostage-taking and attacks on civilians from 7 October 2023. The prosecutor had applied for the warrants on 20 May 2024. Israel, not an ICC member, rejected the court's jurisdiction; Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International welcomed the warrants.

perspectives.framing: Denounced the warrants as antisemitic and politically motivated, rejected the court's jurisdiction over Israel, drew a sharp distinction between a democracy defending itself and a 'terrorist organisation', and vowed to appeal.
Welcomed the warrants against Israeli leaders as an important step toward justice for Palestinians while rejecting the equation of its commanders with them.

President Biden called the warrants outrageous and said there was 'no equivalence' between Israel and Hamas; members of Congress threatened sanctions on the court, which the Trump administration imposed in February 2025.

The court said the judges found reasonable grounds for the charges; many European and other member states said they would respect the court's decision and their legal obligations, while some declined to say whether they would arrest Netanyahu.

title: Israel–Hezbollah ceasefire takes effect in Lebanon
summary: A US- and French-brokered cessation of hostilities between Israel and Hezbollah took effect at 04:00 local time (02:00 GMT) on 27 November 2024, ending more than 13 months of cross-border conflict that had escalated into full-scale war in September. The agreement set a 60-day period in which Israeli forces were to withdraw from southern Lebanon, Hezbollah was to move its fighters and weapons north of the Litani River, about 40 kilometres from the border, and the Lebanese army was to deploy in the south, on the basis of Security Council resolution 1701 (2006); Israel said it retained freedom to act against emerging threats. Governments worldwide welcomed the truce while doubting its durability, per NPR. Lebanon's health ministry counted 3,768 killed and 15,699 injured since 8 October 2023 as of 25 November (UN OCHA), and more than 3,961 killed by the ceasefire (Human Rights Watch).

perspectives.framing: Presented the deal as a victory that pushed Hezbollah from the border and freed Israel to focus on Iran and Gaza, stressing that it retained full freedom of military action against any violation and that the ceasefire's length depended on Hezbollah's conduct.
Claimed a 'divine victory' for having withstood Israel, said it would remain vigilant against violations, and framed its acceptance as protecting Lebanon rather than abandoning Gaza.

Welcomed the ceasefire as a step toward restoring state authority in the south through the army's deployment, demanded full Israeli withdrawal, and documented Israeli strikes after the truce as violations.

The Secretary-General welcomed the announcement and urged full and swift implementation, while the Special Coordinator warned that selective implementation of resolution 1701 'under the guise of ostensible calm' would not suffice.

location: Mount Hermon and the Golan buffer zone, Syria
title: Assad government falls; Israel advances into Syrian buffer zone and Mount Hermon
summary: On 8 December 2024 opposition forces led by Hayat Tahrir al-Sham entered Damascus and President Bashar al-Assad fled to Russia, ending five decades of Assad family rule. The same day Israeli ground forces moved from the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights into the UN-patrolled area of separation established under the 1974 disengagement agreement, taking positions including the Syrian side of Mount Hermon; Israel told the Security Council the measures were 'limited and temporary'. Over the following days the Israeli air force and navy carried out more than 350 strikes on Syrian military assets, which the IDF said destroyed an estimated 70 to 80 per cent of the former regime's strategic military capabilities. Defence Minister Israel Katz said he had ordered a 'sterile defence zone' in southern Syria without a permanent Israeli presence. The UN Secretary-General's spokesperson said the Israeli presence in the buffer zone violated the disengagement agreement.

perspectives.framing: Said the 1974 agreement had collapsed with the Syrian army's abandonment of its positions, that the deployment was a temporary, defensive measure to prevent hostile forces reaching the border, and that the Golan Heights would remain part of Israel 'for eternity'.

Condemned Israel's incursion and strikes as a violation of Syrian sovereignty and the 1974 agreement, said Syria did not seek conflict with Israel, and appealed for international pressure for an Israeli withdrawal.

The Secretary-General called on Syrians to seize a historic opportunity for an inclusive transition; his spokesperson said the UN continued to regard the Golan Heights as occupied territory and that the IDF's occupation of the buffer zone violated the disengagement agreement.
Criticised the Israeli deployment, with France demanding withdrawal from the buffer area and Germany warning Israel and Turkey not to jeopardise the chances of a peaceful transition in Syria.

title: Gaza ceasefire and hostage deal announced; takes effect on 19 January
summary: On 15 January 2025 Qatar, Egypt and the United States announced that Israel and Hamas had agreed a phased ceasefire and hostage-release deal. Its first phase, one of three 42-day phases, provided for the release of 33 Israeli hostages, beginning with three women, in exchange for Palestinian prisoners, a halt to fighting and increased aid, with talks on a second phase intended to end the war. The ceasefire took effect on 19 January, when Hamas released Romi Gonen, Emily Damari and Doron Steinbrecher and Israel freed 90 Palestinian prisoners and detainees from Ofer prison. Gaza's health ministry counted 46,913 Palestinians killed since October 2023 as of that day; an independent survey later estimated about 75,200 violent deaths to 5 January (The Lancet Global Health). Israel publishes no cumulative total; the IDF claimed about 17,000 Hamas fighters killed as of July 2024 (The Jerusalem Post).

perspectives.framing: Presented the deal as securing the hostages' return from a position of strength while reserving the right to resume fighting if Hamas violated it, and stressed that Hamas's destruction remained a war aim; far-right ministers opposed the agreement.

Described the agreement as the fruit of Palestinian 'steadfastness' and 'resistance', an Israeli failure to achieve its goals by force, and demanded full withdrawal and a permanent end to the war in later phases.

Qatar and Egypt framed the deal as a humanitarian breakthrough requiring good-faith implementation; both the outgoing Biden administration and incoming Trump administration claimed credit for the pressure that produced it.

Welcomed the agreement, urged the parties to honour it, and emphasised the need for unimpeded humanitarian access and the release of all hostages, noting that a stray bullet had hit a Red Crescent ambulance days earlier.

title: Phase-one hostage and prisoner exchanges under the January deal
summary: Between 19 January and 1 March 2025 Hamas and Israel carried out weekly exchanges under the first phase of the Gaza ceasefire, with the Red Cross transferring hostages out of Gaza and Palestinian prisoners freed from Ofer prison in the Israeli-occupied West Bank. Hamas staged public handover ceremonies that Israel condemned as humiliating, and on 22 February, after six hostages were handed over, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office delayed the release of more than 600 prisoners who had already boarded buses; Hamas called this a blatant violation of the deal. By the end of the phase on 1 March, Hamas had released the 25 living hostages on the list and the bodies of eight others, and Israel had freed roughly 1,700 to 1,800 Palestinian prisoners and detainees, according to tallies reported by CNN, NBC News and PBS. The sides then deadlocked over extending phase one versus starting phase two.

perspectives.framing: Emphasised the return of hostages, condemned Hamas's 'humiliating' ceremonies and the condition of some captives as violations, and used the delay of prisoner releases as leverage, while calling many of those freed convicted 'terrorists'.

Staged the handovers as displays of continued strength, accused Israel of breaching the deal on aid and withdrawals, and described the freed Palestinians as heroes of the 'resistance' returning from occupation prisons.
Welcomed the releases as a national achievement, while noting Israeli restrictions on celebrations and raids on families' homes reported during the exchanges.
Qatar and Egypt said they were intensifying efforts to salvage the ceasefire when disputes arose; the ICRC, which transferred the hostages and prisoners, called for dignified, private handovers.

title: Operation Iron Wall in Jenin and northern West Bank camps
summary: On 21 January 2025, two days after the Gaza ceasefire began, Israeli forces launched a large-scale operation named 'Iron Wall' in Jenin and its refugee camp, later extending it to the Tulkarm, Nur Shams and Far'a camps. The Palestinian health ministry reported seven people killed and 35 wounded on the first day (Haaretz reported at least nine killed); Israel described the operation as counter-terrorism against armed networks. It involved helicopter fire, air strikes and, in February, the first deployment of tanks in the West Bank since the early 2000s. By 10 February UNRWA estimated that more than 40,000 Palestinians had been displaced from the four camps, the largest displacement in the Israeli-occupied West Bank since 1967. UN OCHA counted 126 Palestinians, including 23 children, killed by Israeli forces across the West Bank between 21 January and 30 June, and Israeli forces remained in the emptied camps, demolishing homes, into mid-2025.

perspectives.framing: Described a counter-terrorism operation in 'Judea and Samaria' against Iranian-backed armed groups entrenched in the camps, said troops would stay for as long as needed and that camp residents were evacuated for their safety, and denied a policy of forced displacement.
Condemned the operation and demolitions as collective punishment and a step toward annexation, while noting that its own security forces had fought armed groups in Jenin camp in the preceding weeks.
Hamas, Islamic Jihad and the Jenin Brigades framed the fighting as resistance to occupation and accused the Palestinian Authority of coordinating with Israel.

OCHA and UNRWA warned of the danger to civilians, damage to roads, water and power, and the largest displacement in the West Bank since 1967, and called on Israel to end unlawful use of force and allow residents to return.

title: Trump proposes US 'ownership' of Gaza and relocation of its population
summary: On 4 February 2025, at a White House press conference with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, US President Donald Trump said the United States would 'take over' the Gaza Strip, clear its rubble and redevelop it as the 'Riviera of the Middle East', with Gaza's roughly two million Palestinians relocated to Egypt, Jordan or elsewhere. Netanyahu called the idea something that 'could change history'. Egypt and Jordan firmly rejected any transfer, as did Saudi Arabia and other Arab states, and Hamas denounced the plan. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres said the next day that it was essential 'to avoid any form of ethnic cleansing'. Arab leaders then held an emergency summit in Cairo on 4 March that adopted an Egyptian plan to rebuild Gaza over five years at a cost of about 53 billion dollars without displacing its population; the United States and Israel rejected it.

perspectives.framing: Cast Gaza as an uninhabitable 'demolition site' whose residents would be better off elsewhere, and the proposal as a bold, generous real-estate and security solution; aides later said relocation would be temporary and voluntary.
Netanyahu called it a remarkable idea worth pursuing; far-right ministers hailed it as endorsing 'voluntary emigration' from Gaza.

Hamas, the Palestinian Authority, Egypt, Jordan and Saudi Arabia rejected the plan as forced displacement and ethnic cleansing, insisted Palestinians would not leave their land, and advanced an Arab reconstruction plan instead.

The Secretary-General said solutions must not make problems worse, that it was vital to stay true to international law and essential to avoid any form of ethnic cleansing, and reaffirmed the two-State solution.

title: Israeli withdrawal deadline in Lebanon passes; troops hold five positions
summary: On 18 February 2025 the extended deadline for Israeli forces to withdraw from southern Lebanon under the November 2024 ceasefire expired. Israeli troops pulled out of the last border towns and villages they had captured, allowing displaced residents to return to largely ruined communities, and the Lebanese army, coordinating with the ceasefire committee and UNIFIL, deployed in 11 villages in the eastern and central sectors. Israel announced, however, that it would keep troops at five 'strategic points' on hilltops overlooking the frontier, including Hamames hill, Labbouneh, Jabal Blat and Jal al-Deir, until satisfied that Hezbollah could not redeploy. President Joseph Aoun, the prime minister and the parliamentary speaker declared any Israeli presence on Lebanese soil an occupation and asked the United States and France, the guarantors, to press for full withdrawal. The UN Special Coordinator and UNIFIL commander called the incomplete withdrawal a violation of resolution 1701.

perspectives.framing: Said the five positions were a temporary security buffer required because the Lebanese army had not yet fully disarmed Hezbollah, and that it would continue to strike any Hezbollah threat anywhere in Lebanon under the ceasefire's terms.

President Aoun and Prime Minister Salam called the remaining positions an occupation and violation of the agreement, and pressed the United States and France, as guarantors, to secure a complete withdrawal.
Said any Israeli presence was an occupation that the Lebanese state must end by all means, while stopping short of resuming attacks.

The Special Coordinator and UNIFIL commander jointly urged both parties to meet their obligations so that safety could be restored to communities on both sides of the Blue Line, and reported continuing Lebanese army deployment.

title: Israel halts entry of all goods and aid into Gaza
summary: On 2 March 2025, the day after the first phase of the Gaza ceasefire expired, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office announced that 'the entry of all goods and supplies to the Gaza Strip will be halted', accusing Hamas of refusing a proposal by US envoy Steve Witkoff to extend the first phase through Ramadan and Passover, with half the remaining hostages released on its first day, rather than proceeding to the second phase. Trucks at the Kerem Shalom crossing returned empty, and the halt covered food, medicine, fuel and cooking gas for about 2.1 million people. Hamas called the decision 'cheap extortion' and a war crime; Egypt rejected 'the politicization of humanitarian aid' and Qatar condemned 'the use of food as a weapon of war'. UN emergency relief coordinator Tom Fletcher called the decision alarming, while Israel called it lawful pressure on Hamas. The closure lasted about eleven weeks.

perspectives.framing: Said Hamas had refused the US 'Witkoff' extension framework, that enough aid had entered during phase one to last for months, that Hamas was diverting supplies, and that halting entry was legitimate leverage rather than a weapon against civilians.
Called the halt a war crime and 'cheap blackmail', accused Israel of violating the ceasefire, and demanded implementation of the second phase as agreed.
Condemned the use of humanitarian aid as a bargaining tool and said there was no alternative to the original agreement.

The Secretary-General urged all parties to prevent a return to hostilities and called for aid to flow immediately; the emergency relief coordinator called Israel's decision alarming and said international humanitarian law is clear that access must be allowed.

title: US air campaign against the Houthis in Yemen
summary: On 15 March 2025 the United States began large-scale air and naval strikes on Houthi targets across Yemen. President Donald Trump said the US would use 'overwhelming lethal force' until the Houthis stopped attacking shipping in the Red Sea; the Houthis had announced a resumption of attacks on Israeli-linked ships after Israel halted aid to Gaza. The Houthis initially said nine civilians had been killed; the Houthi-run health ministry's toll rose to at least 31 and then at least 53 killed with about 100 wounded, and the movement vowed to respond against US warships and Israel. Strikes continued for 51 days, until 6 May, when Trump announced that the Houthis 'don't want to fight any more' and Oman confirmed it had brokered an understanding under which neither side would target the other in the Red Sea; Israel was not covered.

perspectives.framing: Framed the campaign as restoring freedom of navigation and deterring Iran's proxy, warned Tehran that it would be held responsible for Houthi attacks, and later presented the Oman-brokered halt as the Houthis 'capitulating'.

Described the strikes as US-Israeli aggression and war crimes against Yemeni civilians, said its blockade was in solidarity with Gaza and would continue against Israel, and claimed to have forced the United States to stop.
Denied directing the Houthis, condemned the US strikes as a violation of Yemen's sovereignty and the UN Charter, and warned it would respond decisively to any attack on Iran.
Welcomed US action against a 'terrorist' proxy but stressed that Israel would act alone against Houthi attacks on its territory, striking Yemeni ports and airport infrastructure.

title: Israeli strikes across Gaza end the two-month ceasefire
summary: In the early hours of 18 March 2025 Israel launched waves of air strikes across the Gaza Strip, ending the ceasefire that had held since 19 January. Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said he had ordered 'strong action' after Hamas refused to release more hostages or extend the first phase; the White House said Israel had consulted President Trump, and Netanyahu said negotiations would now 'take place only under fire'. Gaza's health ministry reported at least 404 killed and 562 wounded that day (Al Jazeera), with Western outlets reporting more than 400 dead; its cumulative count reached 50,021 on 23 March. Israel publishes no cumulative total; the IDF had claimed about 17,000 Hamas fighters killed as of July 2024, later lowered to about 15,000 (The Jerusalem Post). On 19 March two UN guesthouses in Deir al-Balah were hit, killing one UNOPS staff member.

perspectives.framing: Said the strikes were a response to Hamas's refusal to release hostages and its rearming during the truce, that they targeted Hamas commanders and terrorist infrastructure, and that fighting would continue with increasing force until all hostages were returned.
Accused Israel of unilaterally overturning the agreement, called the strikes 'massacres' against sleeping civilians during Ramadan, and blamed the United States for enabling the return to war.
The Trump administration said it had been consulted, blamed Hamas for rejecting extension proposals, and backed Israel's decision.

The Secretary-General expressed shock at the strikes and hundreds of reported deaths, appealed for the ceasefire to be respected, and condemned the strike on UN premises that killed a UNOPS staff member.

title: Houthi ballistic missile strikes near Ben Gurion Airport
summary: On the morning of 4 May 2025 a ballistic missile launched from Yemen by the Houthi movement evaded Israeli Arrow and US THAAD interceptors and struck beside Terminal 3 of Ben Gurion Airport, Israel's main international gateway, leaving a crater and a plume of smoke. Israel's Magen David Adom said four people were lightly wounded (other reports counted six); the Airports Authority halted flights for about an hour, after which Lufthansa, Delta, Air France and other foreign airlines suspended services to Tel Aviv. The Houthis claimed the strike as support for Gaza and Israel vowed 'strong action'. On 5 May Israeli aircraft struck Hodeidah port, killing at least one person and wounding 35, and on 6 May Sanaa international airport, killing at least three (Houthi-affiliated Al Masirah TV); Defence Minister Israel Katz threatened a naval and aerial blockade. The attack came as Israel's security cabinet approved an expanded Gaza offensive.

perspectives.framing: Claimed a successful hypersonic strike on the 'Zionist entity's' main airport in support of Gaza, declared an air blockade on Israel and urged airlines to stay away.

Called the strike an Iranian-backed terrorist attack that air defences had failed to stop, vowed a sevenfold response, and struck Houthi-controlled ports and Sanaa airport, warning that Iran was responsible for its proxy.
Continued its own campaign against the Houthis but days later announced an Oman-brokered halt covering US ships, saying the Houthis had agreed not to attack American vessels.

title: Operation Gideon's Chariots: Israel launches expanded Gaza offensive
summary: On 17 May 2025 the Israel Defense Forces announced the first stage of 'Gideon's Chariots', an expanded ground and air offensive across northern and southern Gaza that the security cabinet had approved on 4 May, intended to seize and hold territory, dismantle Hamas and secure the release of the remaining hostages. Heavy strikes accompanied the advance: Gaza health authorities reported at least 144 people killed in 24 hours on 17 to 18 May and at least 464 in the preceding week (Al Jazeera), while rescuers told the BBC at least 300 had been killed since 15 May. Gaza's health ministry counted 53,272 killed since October 2023 as of 17 May; Israel publishes no cumulative total, and the IDF had claimed about 17,000 Hamas fighters killed as of July 2024 (The Jerusalem Post). On 19 May Israel allowed limited aid in after eleven weeks.

perspectives.framing: Described a decisive operation to achieve all war aims, defeat Hamas, seize and hold territory, separate civilians from Hamas by moving them to 'humanitarian zones' in the south, and bring the hostages home, while announcing limited aid entry to avert famine.

Called the offensive a campaign of extermination and forced displacement, said no hostages would be released without an end to the war and full withdrawal, and offered partial releases for a 60-day truce.

OCHA reported that air and ground operations were dismantling the means of survival for 2.1 million people, that displacement orders now covered over 40 per cent of the Strip, and that the entire population faced the risk of famine.

Britain, France, Canada and others condemned the expansion and aid restrictions as 'egregious', Arab League states meeting in Baghdad called for an immediate ceasefire, and some governments used the term 'ethnic cleansing'.

title: Gaza Humanitarian Foundation begins aid distribution; deaths near aid sites
summary: On 27 May 2025 the Gaza Humanitarian Foundation (GHF), a US- and Israeli-backed private mechanism, began distributing food at points in Rafah and Deir al-Balah, replacing UN-led distribution that Israel said Hamas had diverted. Thousands of Palestinians stormed the Rafah site on the first day; the Israeli military acknowledged warning shots outside the compound. The UN and major aid agencies refused to take part. On 1 June local health officials and medics reported at least 31 killed and 170 wounded by gunfire about 800 metres from the Tal al-Sultan site; the Israeli military said troops fired warning shots and then at individuals who advanced towards them, and GHF disputed accounts of shootings at its sites. By 27 June the UN human rights office had recorded 613 killings at aid sites and near convoys, 509 near GHF points; Gaza's health ministry counted more than 650.

perspectives.framing: Presented the foundation as a way to feed Gazans while preventing Hamas from looting and profiting from aid, said millions of meals were distributed, denied that its sites were scenes of shootings, and said troops fired warning shots at individuals who approached them in a threatening manner.
Backed and later funded GHF as an innovative solution, blamed Hamas for violence near the sites and criticised the UN for refusing to cooperate.

Called the scheme a militarised distraction from the UN's principled plan, said it forced starving people to walk through combat zones and could not meet needs, and the Secretary-General condemned the reported killings of people seeking aid as unacceptable.
Called the sites 'death traps' and 'humiliation', accused Israel of using hunger as a weapon, and published daily tallies of aid seekers killed.

title: Israel–Iran war: twelve days of strikes end in a US-announced ceasefire
summary: Before dawn on 13 June 2025 Israel launched 'Operation Rising Lion', striking over 100 nuclear and military targets across Iran, including the Natanz enrichment site, and killing top commanders including armed forces chief Mohammad Bagheri and nuclear scientists including Fereydoon Abbasi-Davani. Iran responded with waves of ballistic missiles and drones at Israeli cities. The United States joined on 22 June with strikes on three nuclear sites, and Iran fired missiles at the US Al Udeid base in Qatar on 23 June. A ceasefire announced by President Donald Trump took effect on 24 June, after a final Iranian strike on Beersheba. Iran's health ministry reported 610 killed as of 24 June (later raised to more than 900) and the monitoring group HRANA at least 974; Israeli authorities reported 28 killed and more than 3,000 wounded from about 550 ballistic missiles and 1,000 drones (The Times of Israel).

perspectives.framing: Called the campaign a pre-emptive operation against an existential nuclear and missile threat, said it had set Iran's nuclear programme back years and degraded its missile forces, and declared its goals achieved.

Denounced the strikes as an unprovoked act of war and 'aggression' by the 'Zionist regime' and the United States during nuclear talks, framed its missile barrages as legitimate self-defence, and claimed victory in an 'imposed war'.
President Trump backed Israel, struck Iran's nuclear sites, then brokered and announced the ceasefire, calling it the end of the '12 Day War' and pressing both sides not to violate it.

The Secretary-General condemned military escalation, was particularly concerned by attacks on nuclear installations while US-Iran talks were under way, called for maximum restraint, and welcomed the ceasefire.

title: United States strikes Iranian nuclear sites at Fordow, Natanz and Isfahan
summary: In the early hours of 22 June 2025 (Iran time) the United States entered the Israel-Iran war directly in 'Operation Midnight Hammer': B-2 stealth bombers dropped 14 GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator bombs on the deeply buried Fordow enrichment plant and on Natanz, while a submarine fired more than two dozen Tomahawk cruise missiles at Isfahan. President Donald Trump declared the sites 'obliterated'. IAEA Director General Rafael Grossi told the Security Council that craters were visible at Fordow but no one could yet assess the underground damage, and that inspectors needed to verify Iran's stockpile of more than 400 kg of 60 per cent enriched uranium. UN Secretary-General Antonio Guterres called the bombing 'a perilous turn'. On 23 June Iran's parliament voted to suspend cooperation with the IAEA and Iran fired about 14 ballistic missiles at Al Udeid air base in Qatar.

perspectives.framing: Described a spectacular, one-off success that obliterated Iran's key enrichment sites, removed a nuclear threat and created the conditions for peace, while insisting it did not seek regime change or a wider war.

Called the strikes a flagrant violation of the UN Charter, the NPT and IAEA safeguards, reserved 'all options' for self-defence, and struck the US base in Qatar in a telegraphed response; parliament moved to suspend IAEA cooperation.
Praised the strikes as a historic decision that completed its own campaign against Iran's nuclear programme.

The Secretary-General warned of a 'rathole of retaliation' and said Iran must respect the NPT while all states must act within the Charter; the IAEA reported severe damage but could not verify the fate of enriched uranium and called for inspectors' access.

title: Houthis sink the Magic Seas and Eternity C in the Red Sea
summary: In the first week of July 2025 Houthi forces sank two commercial bulk carriers in the Red Sea, roughly 100 kilometres southwest of the Yemeni port of Hodeidah. The Liberian-flagged, Greek-operated Magic Seas was attacked on 6 July and sank; its crew were rescued. The Eternity C was attacked from 7 July with rocket-propelled grenades fired from small craft and, by the Houthis' own account, missiles and an unmanned boat, and sank on 9 July. Per CNN, citing the operator, three crew members were killed and ten rescued; the EU naval mission put the dead at at least four with others missing, and several crew were taken by the Houthis, which the United States described as kidnapping. The Houthis said they targeted vessels linked to Israel and would continue until the Gaza war ended; Human Rights Watch called the attacks apparent war crimes.

perspectives.framing: Present the sinkings as part of their maritime campaign in support of Gaza, saying the ships belonged to companies dealing with Israeli ports and that the crew members taken aboard were 'rescued'.
Condemned the attacks as unprovoked aggression against commercial shipping and described the seizure of surviving crew as kidnapping, calling for their immediate release.
Framed the attacks as evidence that the Iran-backed Houthis remained a threat to international navigation and cited them in justifying continued Israeli strikes on Houthi targets in Yemen.
Characterised the deliberate attacks on civilian cargo ships and the killing of sailors as apparent war crimes and urged accountability.

title: Lebanese cabinet tasks the army with a plan to disarm Hezbollah
summary: On 5 August 2025 Lebanon's cabinet, under President Joseph Aoun and Prime Minister Nawaf Salam, instructed the Lebanese Armed Forces to draw up a plan by the end of the year to bring all weapons in the country under state control, a direct challenge to Hezbollah, which had refused to disarm after its 2024 war with Israel. On 7 August the cabinet approved the objectives of a paper submitted by US envoy Thomas Barrack that included a disarmament timetable; ministers from Hezbollah and its ally Amal walked out of both sessions. Hezbollah leader Naim Qassem called the decision a 'grave sin' and said the group would not disarm while Israeli forces remained in Lebanon. On 5 September the cabinet 'welcomed' the army's confidential plan without setting a timeframe, the army cautioning that its capabilities were limited. Israel welcomed the decision as a step toward Lebanese sovereignty.

perspectives.framing: Presents the decision as restoring the state's monopoly on arms and implementing the November 2024 ceasefire and UN Security Council Resolution 1701, while seeking Israeli withdrawal and an end to strikes in return.

Rejects disarmament as serving Israeli and American dictates, calls the cabinet decision a 'grave sin' and insists its weapons are the 'resistance' needed while Israel occupies Lebanese territory and continues attacks.
Envoy Thomas Barrack's paper framed disarmament with a timetable as the path to Israeli withdrawal, reconstruction aid and stability; Washington pressed Beirut for a public commitment.
Welcomed the plan as key to Lebanese sovereignty while stating that it would continue to act against Hezbollah's rearmament until disarmament was implemented.

title: Israeli security cabinet approves plan to take control of Gaza City
summary: In the early hours of 8 August 2025 Israel's security cabinet approved Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's proposal for the IDF to take control of Gaza City, the largest urban centre in the Strip, with civilians to be evacuated southward. The government set five conditions for ending the war: disarmament of Hamas, the return of all living and dead hostages, demilitarisation of Gaza, Israeli security control, and a civilian administration that was neither Hamas nor the Palestinian Authority. IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir had warned that the plan would endanger the hostages and stretch the military, and hostage families protested in Tel Aviv and Jerusalem. Britain's prime minister Keir Starmer said the decision was wrong and urged reconsideration, and Turkey called on the UN Security Council to prevent its implementation. The decision set the stage for the Gaza City ground offensive launched in September.

perspectives.framing: Described the plan as the way to 'defeat Hamas' and free the hostages, insisting Israel did not intend to govern Gaza permanently but to hand it to a non-Hamas civilian administration after the war.
The chief of staff and the Hostages and Missing Families Forum warned that an assault on Gaza City would endanger the remaining hostages and exhaust reservists, calling instead for a negotiated deal.
Prime Minister Starmer called the decision wrong, said it would not end the conflict or bring the hostages home, and urged Israel to reconsider.
Condemned the plan in the strongest terms as a step toward occupation and called on the international community and UN Security Council to act.

title: IPC confirms famine in Gaza Governorate
summary: On 22 August 2025 the Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC) confirmed Famine (IPC Phase 5) in Gaza Governorate as of 15 August, the first famine officially confirmed in the Middle East, and projected its spread to Deir al-Balah and Khan Younis governorates by the end of September. The analysis found more than 500,000 people across the Strip facing catastrophic conditions, a further 1.07 million in Emergency (Phase 4) and 396,000 in Crisis (Phase 3), after 22 months of war and restrictions on aid. The WHO and UN Secretary-General António Guterres called the famine man-made and 'a failure of humanity', demanding an immediate ceasefire and unimpeded aid. Israel's Foreign Ministry and COGAT rejected the report as fabricated and based on partial sources affiliated with Hamas, saying there was no famine in Gaza and citing increased aid deliveries. In December the IPC assessed that famine conditions no longer prevailed.

perspectives.framing: Presented the finding as a technical, evidence-based classification and described the famine as entirely man-made and preventable, calling for a ceasefire and full humanitarian access.

The Foreign Ministry and COGAT called the report 'fabricated' and 'methodologically flawed', said it relied on Hamas-affiliated data, asserted that there was no famine and pointed to aid volumes entering the Strip.
Cited the confirmation as proof of a deliberate policy of starvation and a 'crime of genocide', demanding international intervention to open crossings.
Commissioner Hadja Lahbib said the confirmation was a man-made catastrophe and called on Israel to allow immediate, unimpeded humanitarian access.

title: Strike on Nasser Hospital kills 20-22 people including five journalists
summary: On the morning of 25 August 2025 Israeli tank fire struck an upper floor and external staircase of Nasser Hospital in Khan Younis in two rounds minutes apart; the second hit rescuers and journalists who had rushed to the site after the first. Per the Gaza Health Ministry 20 people were killed, while Civil Defence and hospital officials cited by CNN and AP put the toll at 22 with about 50 wounded, including five journalists: Reuters cameraman Hussam al-Masri, AP freelancer Mariam Dagga, Al Jazeera's Mohammed Salama, freelancer Moaz Abu Taha and Ahmed Abu Aziz of Middle East Eye. Netanyahu called it a 'tragic mishap'; an initial IDF inquiry on 26 August said troops had targeted a camera it said Hamas placed to observe forces and that six of the dead were militants; the chief of staff ordered a wider probe into the authorisation and munitions used.

perspectives.framing: Called the deaths a 'tragic mishap', said the target was a Hamas surveillance camera on the hospital roof, identified six of the dead as 'terrorists' and said the strike's approval process and munitions would be investigated.
Described the strike as a deliberate 'massacre' of journalists and rescuers and part of a pattern of attacks on hospitals and the press.
Reuters, AP and Al Jazeera demanded explanations; the Committee to Protect Journalists and others called the 'double-tap' strike an attack on the press and demanded accountability.
The Secretary-General condemned the killing of journalists and health workers and called for a prompt, impartial investigation and respect for the protection of hospitals.

title: Israeli air strike targets Hamas leadership in Doha
summary: On 9 September 2025 Israeli aircraft struck a residential compound in the Leqtaifiya district of Doha where Hamas's political leadership was meeting to discuss a US ceasefire proposal. According to Israeli officials cited by CNN, more than ten jets fired over ten munitions at a target list that included chief negotiator Khalil al-Hayya, Zaher Jabarin, Muhammad Darwish and Khaled Mashal. Hamas said five of its members were killed, including al-Hayya's son and his office director, but that the negotiating delegation survived; Qatar said a member of its Internal Security Force was also killed. It was Israel's first known strike in Qatar, a US ally, and its first on a Gulf Cooperation Council member. Qatar condemned the attack as a violation of its sovereignty and suspended its mediation; on 29 September Netanyahu apologised to Qatar's prime minister in a call arranged by President Trump.

perspectives.framing: Said it acted alone against the 'terrorist leadership' responsible for 7 October, that the targets were legitimate wherever they hid, and later expressed regret to Qatar for the death of a Qatari serviceman.
Condemned a 'cowardly' and 'treacherous' attack on a sovereign state hosting negotiations it was conducting at US request, and demanded international accountability.
Called the strike a failed assassination attempt that proved Israel was not seeking a deal, while confirming that the delegation survived and five members were killed.
President Trump said he was unhappy with the strike, that it did not advance US or Israeli goals, and that Qatar was a strong ally; he later brokered Netanyahu's apology.

title: Israeli ground offensive in Gaza City (Gideon's Chariots II)
summary: On 16 September 2025 elements of three IDF divisions, the 98th, 162nd and 36th, pushed into Gaza City in the ground phase of Operation Gideon's Chariots II, after two weeks of air strikes on high-rise buildings and after the military placed the entire city, home to an estimated one million people, under an evacuation order directing residents to Al-Mawasi. Defence Minister Israel Katz declared that 'Gaza is burning'. By mid-September the IDF said it controlled about 40 percent of the city. UN OCHA, citing the Site Management Cluster, recorded more than 388,400 displacement movements between 14 August and 23 September, roughly 9,700 a day, as hundreds of thousands moved south along the coastal road while many others remained. Amnesty International described a catastrophic wave of mass displacement under inhumane conditions. The offensive halted when the ceasefire took effect on 10 October and Israeli forces withdrew to the Yellow Line.

perspectives.framing: Framed the operation as the decisive phase to dismantle Hamas's last stronghold and free the hostages, saying civilians were warned and given a humanitarian zone in the south.
Described the assault as a war of extermination and forced displacement, and said Israel bore responsibility for the fate of hostages held in the city.
Reported that nearly one million people in a famine-affected city faced bombardment and impossible evacuation conditions, and said the south lacked space, shelter and services for new arrivals.
Characterised the evacuation orders and destruction as forced displacement and part of what it called genocide, calling for an immediate halt to the offensive.

title: UN Commission of Inquiry concludes Israel committed genocide in Gaza
summary: On 16 September 2025 the Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory, a three-member body established by the UN Human Rights Council and chaired by Navi Pillay, published a report concluding that Israeli authorities and security forces had committed genocide against Palestinians in the Gaza Strip between 7 October 2023 and 31 July 2025. It found four of the five acts listed in the 1948 Genocide Convention: killing, causing serious bodily or mental harm, inflicting conditions of life calculated to destroy the group, and imposing measures intended to prevent births, and inferred intent from statements by Israeli civilian and military leaders and the pattern of military conduct. The paper (A/HRC/60/CRP.3) was presented to the Council's 60th session. Israel's Foreign Ministry rejected the report as 'distorted and false' and accused the panel of echoing Hamas propaganda; Amnesty International said the finding must spur international action.

perspectives.framing: Presented its conclusion as a legal finding under the Genocide Convention based on two years of evidence, and called on states to prevent genocide and to end arms transfers.
Rejected the report as 'distorted and false', called the commissioners biased 'Hamas proxies', and said Israel was fighting a defensive war in accordance with international law.
Welcomed the finding as confirmation of what Palestinians had described since 2023 and demanded sanctions and prosecutions.
Amnesty International and others said the report aligned with their own findings and urged governments to act on their obligations under the Convention.
