title: UK, Canada, Australia, France and others recognise the State of Palestine
summary: On 21 September 2025 the United Kingdom, Canada and Australia formally recognised the State of Palestine in a coordinated step, with Portugal following the same day. On 22 September, at a UN General Assembly high-level conference on the two-state solution co-chaired by France and Saudi Arabia, President Emmanuel Macron announced France's recognition, joined by Belgium, Luxembourg and Malta. The governments said recognition was intended to preserve the possibility of a two-state solution amid the war in Gaza and settlement expansion, and was tied to Palestinian Authority reform and the exclusion of Hamas from governance. Prime Minister Netanyahu responded that 'there will be no Palestinian state' and said Israel's answer would come after his return from the United States; the United States opposed the move, and some Israeli ministers called for annexing parts of the West Bank. The Palestinian Authority welcomed the recognitions as historic.

perspectives.party: United Kingdom, Canada, Australia and France
perspectives.framing: Framed recognition as keeping alive the two-state solution and rewarding a reformed Palestinian Authority rather than Hamas, while condemning the 7 October attack and calling for the hostages' release.

Called the recognitions a 'reward for terror' after 7 October, vowed that no Palestinian state would be established, and floated sovereignty measures in the West Bank ('Judea and Samaria') in response.
President Mahmoud Abbas welcomed the decisions as a historic step toward realising Palestinian self-determination and urged other states to follow.
Opposed unilateral recognition, said it did nothing to free hostages or end the war, and denied visas to the Palestinian delegation ahead of the General Assembly session.

title: Trump unveils 20-point plan to end the Gaza war
summary: On 29 September 2025 President Donald Trump, appearing with Prime Minister Netanyahu at the White House, unveiled a 20-point 'Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict' that Netanyahu said Israel accepted. The plan provided for an immediate end to fighting once both sides agreed, the return of all living and dead hostages within 72 hours of Israeli acceptance, the release of 250 Palestinian prisoners serving life sentences and 1,700 Gazans detained since 7 October 2023, a staged Israeli withdrawal, disarmament of Hamas with amnesty for members who renounced violence, a technocratic Palestinian committee to run Gaza under an international 'Board of Peace' chaired by Trump, a temporary International Stabilisation Force, and a possible future political horizon for Palestinian self-determination. The White House said the plan was drafted in consultation with Arab and Muslim states. Hamas gave a partial acceptance and indirect talks in Egypt produced the 9 October agreement.

perspectives.framing: Presented the plan as the end of the war, a path to a demilitarised and rebuilt Gaza and to wider regional normalisation, warning that Israel would have US backing to 'finish the job' if Hamas refused.

Netanyahu said the plan met Israel's war aims of disarming Hamas and returning the hostages, stressed that the IDF would stay in most of Gaza until demilitarisation, and rejected any role for the Palestinian Authority without reform.
Accepted the hostage-release and withdrawal provisions in principle but said disarmament and Gaza's future governance were national matters to be decided by Palestinians.

Egypt, Qatar, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Jordan, the UAE, Indonesia and Pakistan welcomed the announcement and pledged to work with Washington on implementation, while stressing eventual Palestinian statehood.

title: Israeli navy intercepts the Global Sumud Flotilla
summary: On the evening of 1 October 2025 the Israeli navy began intercepting the Global Sumud Flotilla, a civilian convoy of roughly 40 to 45 vessels carrying several hundred activists, parliamentarians, doctors and lawyers, among them Swedish campaigner Greta Thunberg, that sought to break the maritime blockade of Gaza and deliver aid. Boarding operations continued through the night into 2 October in international waters as communications were jammed; NPR reported that most vessels were seized and their passengers detained and taken to Israel for deportation, and Al Jazeera reported that the final boat was intercepted on 3 October. Israel described the interception as peaceful and the flotilla as a provocation serving Hamas; Italy said it had received assurances that no violence would be used. Organisers and Front Line Defenders said the seizure in international waters violated international law and that detainees were denied legal counsel; protests followed in several countries.

perspectives.framing: Called the flotilla a 'selfie' publicity stunt and provocation that carried negligible aid, said the naval blockade is lawful, and emphasised that the interception was carried out without violence and participants were deported.
Described a peaceful civilian humanitarian mission to break an illegal siege and said the boarding of ships in international waters and detention of participants amounted to abduction.
Said the interception in international waters violated international law and raised concerns about arbitrary detention and denial of access to lawyers.
Urged restraint and consular protection for their nationals; Italy relayed Israeli assurances of non-violence while Spain and others criticised the interception.

title: Sharm el-Sheikh ceasefire takes effect; IDF withdraws to the Yellow Line
summary: On 9 October 2025 Israel and Hamas agreed the first phase of Trump's plan after indirect talks in Sharm el-Sheikh mediated by Egypt, Qatar, Turkey and the United States; the Israeli cabinet ratified it overnight and the ceasefire took effect at noon on 10 October, when Israeli forces pulled back to a demarcation known as the 'Yellow Line'. Israel completed the withdrawal within 24 hours while retaining direct control of roughly 53 percent of the Strip per Gisha's mapping, including Rafah and the eastern belt; tens of thousands of displaced Palestinians walked north toward Gaza City. The text provided for hostage releases within 72 hours, a prisoner exchange and a surge of aid. On 13 October Trump addressed the Knesset and then joined leaders of more than 20 countries at a Sharm el-Sheikh summit where the US, Egypt, Qatar and Turkey signed a guarantors' declaration; Netanyahu did not attend.

perspectives.framing: President Trump proclaimed the end of the war and 'the historic dawn of a new Middle East', presenting the deal as the first phase of his 20-point plan guaranteed by the US and regional mediators.

Presented the agreement as securing the return of all hostages while the IDF remained deployed in more than half of Gaza until Hamas disarmed; the chief of staff later called the Yellow Line 'a new border line'.
Framed the agreement as ending the war and the 'genocide' and forcing an Israeli withdrawal, while insisting that its weapons and Gaza's governance remained Palestinian matters.

title: Last 20 living hostages freed; Israel releases about 1,968 Palestinians
summary: On 13 October 2025, about 72 hours after the ceasefire took effect, Hamas handed the last 20 living Israeli hostages to the International Committee of the Red Cross in two groups, ending more than two years of captivity, and later that day transferred the bodies of four deceased hostages, out of 28 it was required to return. In exchange Israel released about 1,968 Palestinian prisoners and detainees: 250 serving life sentences, many of whom were transferred to Egypt, and about 1,700 people detained in Gaza since 7 October 2023, who were bused to Ramallah and to Khan Younis. President Trump addressed the Knesset, declaring the war over, before flying to the Sharm el-Sheikh summit. Hamas subsequently returned remains in batches; Israel said several handovers were slow or misidentified, and the bodies of about 360 Palestinians were transferred to Gaza in return over the following weeks.

summary: On 19 October 2025, nine days into the ceasefire, the IDF said its troops in Rafah, east of the Yellow Line, came under anti-tank and sniper fire; two soldiers, Maj. Yaniv Kula and Staff Sgt. Itay Yavetz of the Nahal Brigade, were killed and three wounded. Israel responded with what the army called a 'massive and extensive wave' of strikes on dozens of targets across the Strip and briefly halted aid entry. Gaza's Civil Defence agency said at least 42 Palestinians were killed that day, per Al Jazeera, and the Gaza Government Media Office said 97 Palestinians had been killed since the truce began. Hamas's armed wing said it remained committed to the ceasefire and had no contact with fighters trapped in Rafah. Both sides accused the other of violations; US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner flew to Israel the next day and Washington said the ceasefire held.

perspectives.framing: Said Hamas had blatantly violated the ceasefire by attacking soldiers inside the Israeli-controlled zone and that the strikes were a proportionate response to 'terrorist' targets.
Denied ordering any attack, said its fighters in Rafah were cut off from the leadership, and accused Israel of fabricating pretexts to continue killing civilians and to block aid.
Vice President Vance and the envoys said skirmishes were expected, that the ceasefire was holding, and that Hamas would be 'obliterated' if it kept breaching the deal.

title: Israeli strikes kill more than 100 in Gaza's deadliest day since the ceasefire

title: UN Security Council adopts Resolution 2803 on the Board of Peace and ISF
summary: On 17 November 2025 the UN Security Council adopted Resolution 2803 by 13 votes to none, with China and Russia abstaining, endorsing the US 'Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict' agreed by Israel and Hamas in October. The resolution welcomed the Board of Peace, to be chaired by President Trump, as a transitional administration for Gaza overseeing a technocratic Palestinian committee, and authorised member states to form a temporary International Stabilization Force under the Board's unified command to secure borders, protect civilians and aid corridors, and oversee Gaza's demilitarisation and the decommissioning of weapons in coordination with Israel and Egypt, with Israeli forces to withdraw as the force established control. It referred to a possible pathway to Palestinian self-determination and statehood once Palestinian Authority reform and reconstruction advanced. Washington called the vote historic; Russia and China argued the Council had ceded its role; Hamas rejected international guardianship.

perspectives.framing: Presented the resolution as historic international backing for ending the war, disarming Hamas and rebuilding Gaza under the Board of Peace.
Abstained, arguing that the Council was handing Gaza's governance to an unaccountable external body, that the text lacked UN oversight, and that Palestinian statehood was insufficiently guaranteed.
Welcomed the mandate to disarm Hamas and demilitarise Gaza while rejecting the language on a pathway to a Palestinian state.
Rejected the resolution as imposing an international guardianship on Gaza and said disarmament would strip Palestinians of the 'right to resist' occupation.
Welcomed the endorsement and its reference to statehood, and said it was ready to assume responsibility in Gaza after reform.

title: Israeli strike in Beirut kills Hezbollah chief of staff Haytham Ali Tabatabai
summary: On 23 November 2025 an Israeli air strike on an apartment in Beirut's southern suburb of Dahieh killed Haytham Ali Tabatabai, Hezbollah's chief of staff and the most senior figure in the group after Secretary-General Naim Qassem, together with four other members whom Hezbollah named as Qasem Barjawi, Mustafa Barou, Rifaat Hussein and Ibrahim Hussein. It was the first Israeli strike on Beirut in months and the highest-profile killing since the November 2024 ceasefire, which Israel said it was enforcing against Hezbollah's rebuilding of its forces; Netanyahu called Tabatabai a 'mass murderer'. Hezbollah acknowledged the death hours later and described the attack as a flagrant violation of the ceasefire, while Lebanon's government condemned the strike as it pursued its plan for a state monopoly on arms. Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon continued almost daily.

title: Gaza Health Ministry death toll passes 70,000
summary: On 29 November 2025 the Gaza Health Ministry announced that the cumulative death toll since 7 October 2023 had reached 70,100, after 299 previously unregistered deaths were verified, and that 354 Palestinians had been killed by Israeli fire since the ceasefire took effect on 10 October; the ministry's counts do not distinguish civilians from combatants. title: US declares Phase Two of Gaza plan; technocratic committee named
summary: On 14 January 2026 US Special Envoy Steve Witkoff announced, on behalf of President Trump, the launch of Phase Two of the 20-point plan to end the Gaza war, described as a move from ceasefire to demilitarisation, technocratic governance and reconstruction. The same day Qatari, Egyptian and Turkish mediators named former Palestinian minister Ali Shaath as chief commissioner of the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, a transitional technocratic body excluding Hamas and the Palestinian Authority, to be supervised by the Board of Peace with UN envoy Nickolay Mladenov in a guiding role. Witkoff said Washington expected Hamas to comply fully with its obligations, including returning the last deceased hostage. Al Jazeera reported that most Phase One commitments had not materialised: it counted Israeli attacks on 82 of the first 97 ceasefire days, and 23,019 aid trucks entering Gaza by 9 January, about 43 percent of the number envisaged.

perspectives.framing: Presents Phase Two as the transition from ceasefire to 'demilitarization, technocratic governance, and reconstruction' under the President's 20-Point Plan, and warns that Hamas's failure to meet its commitments will bring 'serious consequences'.

Palestinian factions publicly welcomed the transitional committee while Hamas insisted that Israel had not honoured Phase One (aid volumes, crossings, withdrawal lines) and that disarmament demands were premature.

Treats Phase Two as the stage in which Hamas must be fully disarmed and Gaza demilitarised before any further Israeli withdrawal, and stresses the return of the final deceased hostage as a precondition.
Through Security Council Resolution 2803 the UN endorsed the framework; UN officials urged consolidation of the ceasefire, full humanitarian access and restraint by all parties.

title: Trump signs Board of Peace charter with founding members at Davos
summary: On 22 January 2026 President Trump hosted a signing ceremony for the founding charter of the Board of Peace on the sidelines of the World Economic Forum in Davos, formally establishing the body as an international organisation with himself as chairman. Leaders or senior officials from 17 countries, including Argentina's Javier Milei and Hungary's Viktor Orban, were called to the stage as founding members; the House of Commons Library later reported that up to 35 states had agreed to join, none of them other G7 members. The Board, whose members Trump had announced on 17 January, is intended to oversee post-war stabilisation, governance and reconstruction in Gaza and to supervise the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza. Its executive board included Marco Rubio, Tony Blair, Steve Witkoff, Ajay Banga, Jared Kushner, Marc Rowan and Robert Gabriel. The UAE accepted an invitation to join on 21 January.

perspectives.framing: The White House described the ceremony as 'ratifying' the Board of Peace and 'opening a path to hope and dignity for Gazans', presenting the Board as a new international mechanism for stabilising Gaza and potentially other conflict zones.

Several allies stayed outside the Board; commentators such as Foreign Policy framed the initiative as either a Gaza reconstruction vehicle or an attempt to build a parallel structure to the UN.

title: Israel recovers remains of Ran Gvili, last hostage held in Gaza
summary: On 26 January 2026 the Israeli military announced that it had recovered the remains of Ran Gvili, a police officer killed on 7 October 2023 while defending Kibbutz Alumim, from the al-Batesh cemetery in the Shejaiya–Tuffah area of northern Gaza City. Gvili was the last of the 28 deceased hostages whose return was required under the October 2025 ceasefire; his body had been held for 843 days. Israeli forces said they examined around 250 corpses during the recovery operation, and the Shin Bet said the breakthrough came from the capture about a month earlier of an Islamic Jihad operative who knew where the remains had been moved. The return meant that for the first time since 2014 no Israeli hostages, living or dead, were held in Gaza, removing a central dispute over Hamas's Phase One compliance. Gvili's funeral was held in his hometown of Meitar.

title: Rafah crossing with Egypt partially reopens after nearly two years
summary: On 2 February 2026 the Rafah crossing between Gaza and Egypt partially reopened for the first time since Israeli forces seized it in May 2024, in what Israel described as a pilot completing the final step of Phase One of the October 2025 ceasefire. An Israeli security official told CNN that 150 Palestinians a day would be allowed to leave and 50 to enter, but only five medical patients were permitted to exit on the first day. UN News reported hope but also 'massive trepidation' among Gazans over how limited the reopening would be. The crossing is Gaza's only land link to a country other than Israel and is the main route for seriously ill and wounded patients seeking treatment abroad.

title: Israeli cabinet approves West Bank land measures and Area C land registration
summary: On 8 February 2026 Israel's security cabinet adopted a package of decisions substantially increasing Israeli governmental authority in the Israeli-occupied West Bank, easing direct purchase of land by Israelis and opening West Bank land registries to public review. title: US and Israel launch war on Iran; Supreme Leader Khamenei killed
summary: On 28 February 2026 the United States and Israel launched a joint aerial campaign against Iran, named Operation Epic Fury by the US and Operation Roaring Lion by Israel. Britannica records nearly 900 strikes in the first 12 hours on missile sites, air defences, military infrastructure and leadership; Israeli officials told CNN roughly 500 sites were hit. Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei was killed in a strike on his Tehran compound, and Iran declared 40 days of mourning. Iran retaliated with hundreds of ballistic missiles and thousands of drones against Israel and US-linked targets in Gulf states; a 1 March missile strike on Beit Shemesh killed nine Israeli civilians. Iran's Health Ministry, cited by Al Jazeera, reported 3,468 people killed in Iran; The Times of Israel counted 650 Iranian missiles and 24 people killed in Israel and the West Bank. title: Hezbollah joins Iran war; Israel launches air and ground offensive in Lebanon
summary: On 2 March 2026, less than 48 hours after the US-Israeli strikes on Iran and the killing of Ali Khamenei, Hezbollah fired rockets at northern Israel, including a missile-defence site near Haifa, calling the attack a 'defensive act'. Israeli evacuation orders and bombing of southern Lebanon, the Bekaa and Beirut's southern suburbs displaced more than one million people, a fifth of Lebanon's population, according to Al Jazeera and Time. title: US and Iran agree Pakistan-mediated two-week ceasefire
summary: On 8 April 2026, after nearly 40 days of war, President Trump announced on Truth Social a two-week ceasefire between the United States and Iran, mediated by Pakistan's prime minister and army chief, with talks to follow in Islamabad. Pakistan's prime minister said the ceasefire covered 'everywhere, including Lebanon', but the parties disagreed on whether Lebanon was included, and within hours Israel carried out its heaviest strikes of the war on Lebanon. title: Israel and Lebanon begin US-brokered ten-day cessation of hostilities
summary: On 16 April 2026 a US-brokered cessation of hostilities between Israel and Lebanon took effect at 17:00 EST for an initial period of ten days, framed in the State Department text as a goodwill gesture by Israel to enable good-faith negotiations toward a permanent security and peace agreement. title: US and Iran sign 14-point memorandum of understanding to end the war
summary: On 17 June 2026 President Trump and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian signed, remotely, a 14-point memorandum of understanding intended to end the Iran war. Trump signed during a dinner with President Emmanuel Macron at the Palace of Versailles after the G7 summit, and Pezeshkian signed in Tehran. According to the text published by CNN and the Arab Center, the framework provided for an end to military strikes, removal of the US naval blockade of Iranian ports, and Iranian arrangements for the safe passage of commercial vessels through the Strait of Hormuz with no charge for 60 days, with the strait's future administration to be determined by Iran in consultation with Oman and other Gulf states. Al Jazeera later reported that vague wording, particularly Article 5 on who controlled shipping, caused immediate disputes, and the memorandum expired in August without renewal.

perspectives.framing: Presented the memorandum as ending the war on American terms, with the strait reopened toll-free and Iran's nuclear and missile programmes to be addressed in follow-on talks.
Framed the document as recognition of Iranian sovereignty over the Strait of Hormuz and an end to the blockade, reserving the right to regulate shipping after the 60-day period.
Voiced scepticism that the framework constrained Iran's missile and nuclear capabilities and insisted on retaining freedom of action.
Welcomed the reopening of shipping lanes while seeking a role in the strait's future administration and guarantees against further attacks on their territory.

title: Israel–Lebanon framework deal ties withdrawal to Hezbollah disarmament
summary: On 26 June 2026, after four days of US-brokered talks in Washington, Israel and Lebanon agreed a framework to end their months-long conflict. The deal ties Israeli withdrawal to the disarmament of Hezbollah and does not mandate Israeli withdrawal from the roughly one-fifth of Lebanese territory its forces hold. A joint US–Lebanon–Israel statement said the sides would swiftly advance pilot zones in which the Lebanese Armed Forces take exclusive control of territory to the exclusion of all non-state actors. Al Jazeera noted the talks were the first direct negotiations between Israel and the Lebanese government since the failed 1983 May 17 Agreement, and followed a conditional ceasefire agreed on 4 June. Hezbollah, which did not take part, called the agreement 'null and void'. The framework's implementation remained uncertain as of September 2026.

perspectives.framing: Hails the framework as a historic step toward a permanent Israel–Lebanon peace and the restoration of Lebanese state monopoly on arms.
Presents the deal as securing the north by conditioning any withdrawal on verified Hezbollah disarmament, with Israel retaining positions until then.
Describes the agreement as a path to sovereignty and reconstruction, while under domestic pressure over negotiating directly with Israel and over the absence of a withdrawal timetable.
Rejects the agreement as 'null and void', refuses disarmament while Israel occupies Lebanese land, and accuses the government of capitulation.

title: Iran hits ships in Hormuz, US strikes back; Trump declares memorandum 'over'
summary: On 6–7 July 2026 Iranian forces attacked three commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz that had not followed Iran's approved route, in what Tehran presented as an assertion of sovereignty over the waterway. The United States responded from 7 July with retaliatory strikes on dozens of Iranian targets. On 8 July, speaking at the NATO summit in Ankara, President Trump declared the June memorandum of understanding 'over'. Al Jazeera reported the dispute centred on Article 5 of the memorandum, which Washington read as an Iranian obligation not to impede transit and Tehran read as recognising its authority over shipping. On 22 July Trump warned that each further attack on a ship would be answered by destroying a bridge or power plant, including in Tehran. The memorandum formally expired on 17 August without renewal, leaving the April ceasefire in an uneasy state.

perspectives.framing: Casts Iran's ship attacks as violations of the memorandum and of freedom of navigation, and its strikes as holding Iranian forces accountable.
Asserts that the memorandum recognised its role in administering the strait and that vessels ignoring Iranian instructions were lawfully intercepted; describes US strikes as renewed aggression.
Expressed alarm at disruption of oil and gas exports and urged de-escalation and a negotiated shipping regime.
Pointed to the breakdown as vindicating its warnings that Iran would not honour the framework.

title: Knesset dissolves itself; Israeli election set for 27 October 2026
summary: On 17 July 2026 the 25th Knesset voted 62–0, with coalition support including Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu, to dissolve itself and formally set a general election for 27 October 2026, the last date permitted by law; the coalition had announced the date on 12 July. It was the first Knesset since 1988 to complete a full four-year term, and the vote followed what The Times of Israel called a final legislative blitz by the coalition. The election will be the first since the 7 October 2023 attack and is widely described as a referendum on Netanyahu's handling of the wars in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran. Britannica and Haaretz identified Netanyahu's Likud and a bloc led by former chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot as the leading contenders, with neither assured of a coalition.

perspectives.framing: Presents the completed term as proof of stability and campaigns on having removed the Iranian nuclear threat and defeated Hamas and Hezbollah.
Frames the vote as a chance to end Netanyahu's tenure, citing the 7 October failures, hostages, judicial overhaul and the draft-exemption dispute.
Says the outcome matters little unless any Israeli government halts settlement expansion and annexation and accepts a Palestinian state.
Publicly neutral, while the Trump administration has signalled continued support for Netanyahu's regional policies.

title: Israeli cabinet approves International Stabilization Force entry into Gaza
summary: On 26 July 2026 Israel's security cabinet approved in principle the entry of the International Stabilization Force (ISF) envisaged by the 20-point plan and UN Security Council Resolution 2803 into areas of Gaza beyond Israeli control. The decision authorised an initial contingent of up to about 200 personnel for a pilot humanitarian zone near Rafah, subject to approval by the prime minister, defence minister and foreign minister. Reports named Kosovo, Albania and Morocco, with Kazakhstan and Uganda possible contributors. ISF personnel would receive immunity under Israeli law and operate in coordination with the Israeli military outside its control zones. National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir opposed the decision, arguing Hamas had not met its commitments. FDD's Long War Journal described it as the first formal Israeli authorisation of the multinational force nine months after the ceasefire.

perspectives.framing: Presents the approval as a limited, reversible pilot that keeps Israeli security control and immunity arrangements, conditional on Hamas disarmament; far-right ministers call it a reward for Hamas.
Welcomes the decision as unlocking Phase Two deployment and reconstruction in the Rafah pilot zone.
Says it accepts an international force only to monitor a ceasefire and Israeli withdrawal, not to disarm Palestinians, and objects to a force coordinated with the Israeli army.
Insists the force must operate under a UN mandate and in coordination with Palestinian institutions, not as a substitute for Palestinian sovereignty.

title: UN warns West Bank settler violence at all-time high; OCHA logs 1,000+ attacks
summary: On 29 July 2026 UN officials warned that settler violence in the Israeli-occupied West Bank had reached an all-time high. UN OCHA recorded that settler attacks causing casualties or property damage passed 1,000 by 11 June, and more than 1,380 incidents affecting over 250 Palestinian communities by 31 July, an average of about 6.6 per day, the highest pace on record. OCHA counted at least 15 Palestinians, including two children, killed by settlers as of 24 July, approaching its previous annual record of 16 in 2023. Human Rights Watch reported that settler violence, which it described as Israel-backed, displaced more than 6,200 Palestinians, including over 3,000 children, between January 2023 and early July 2026, and warned of a risk of mass atrocities. The trend coincided with the February land-registration decisions and expanded Israeli administrative control.

perspectives.framing: Describes the violence as occurring with impunity and in a context of accelerating annexation, and links it to forcible transfer prohibited under international humanitarian law.

Human Rights Watch characterises settler attacks as state-backed and warns they threaten mass atrocities; B'Tselem and others use the term 'ethnic cleansing' for the displacement of herding communities.

Condemns violence by 'a small minority' of settlers, says police and the army act against it, and rejects characterisations of state backing; some ministers describe settlers as defending communities against Palestinian 'terror'.
Calls the attacks organised terrorism sponsored by the government to empty Area C and demands international protection and sanctions.

title: Board of Peace announces staged Hamas disarmament agreement
summary: On 30 July 2026 President Trump announced that the Board of Peace had reached an agreement on the disarmament of Hamas, and on 31 July the Board and the International Stabilization Force said mediators from Egypt, Qatar, Turkey and the United States had finalised a roadmap for the next phase of the ceasefire. Under the terms reported by Al Jazeera and Euronews, Hamas and other armed factions would hand over weapons in stages to the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza, beginning with police weapons and followed by decommissioning of heavy weapons, with inventories of production sites, depots and the tunnel network, alongside Israeli withdrawal steps. Hamas said it would implement the deal only if Israel met its own ceasefire and withdrawal commitments, and tied full disarmament to a path to statehood. An Israeli minister called the agreement 'unacceptable', and Israel did not publicly endorse it.

perspectives.framing: Trump called it a 'historic' deal for the complete disarmament of Hamas and Israeli withdrawal, presenting it as the core of Phase Two.

Describes the arrangement as 'storing' or transferring weapons to a Palestinian body, not surrender, conditional on Israeli compliance and linked to ending the occupation; its armed wing had earlier called disarmament demands unacceptable.
Divided: officials demand full, verified demilitarisation before any withdrawal, and a cabinet minister publicly rejected the terms as unacceptable.
Present the roadmap as a balanced sequence of disarmament and withdrawal that preserves the ceasefire and Palestinian governance of Gaza.

title: Israeli forces capture Hamas internal security chief in Gaza City raid
summary: On the morning of 1 September 2026 Shin Bet special forces, backed by the Israeli military, captured Muein al-Arabid, head of Hamas's internal security apparatus, in a raid in Gaza City that turned into a firefight; the air force struck nearby targets to cover the ground force and Israel reported no casualties on its side. Prime Minister Netanyahu said the detainee had been responsible for hiding and moving hostages, concealing senior officials and rebuilding Hamas capabilities. FDD's Long War Journal reported that the Israeli military logged 29 Hamas ceasefire violations between 19 August and 3 September. The raid, nearly eleven months into the ceasefire and a month after the disarmament roadmap, illustrated continued Israeli operations beyond its control line. Gaza's Health Ministry put the cumulative death toll since October 2023 at about 73,658 and those killed since the ceasefire at 1,352 in early September; no Israeli cumulative figure was retrieved.

perspectives.framing: Hails the operation as changing the rules of the game in Gaza, showing Israel will act against Hamas leaders anywhere and treats such raids as consistent with the ceasefire's self-defence provisions.

Condemns the raid and accompanying strikes as a flagrant violation of the ceasefire and evidence that Israel is not committed to the agreement, and reiterates that its own obligations depend on Israeli compliance.
Urge restraint and warn that unilateral operations jeopardise the disarmament and withdrawal sequencing agreed in July.
Continues to record deaths, injuries and access restrictions under the ceasefire in its impact snapshots, presenting Ministry of Health and Israeli-authority figures side by side.
